slides.heading: When They Keep Getting Out
slides.body: Stay boring. Walk them back calmly, say 'It's bedtime,' and leave. No negotiation, no cuddles, no anger. The first 3 nights are the hardest. If you stay consistent, most children adjust within a week. You may need to walk them back 30+ times the first night — that's normal!

content.statement: You should transition your toddler to a big bed as soon as they turn 2.
content.explanation: There's no magic age. Most sleep experts recommend waiting until 2.5–3 unless safety requires it sooner (e.g., climbing out of the cot). Early transitions often create more sleep problems.

activities.title: Mealtime Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore toddler feeding, check in with how mealtimes are going.

content.question: How stressful are mealtimes in your household right now?

slides.heading: The Parent's Job
slides.body: You decide WHAT food is served, WHEN meals happen, and WHERE they eat. That's it. You stock the options. You set the schedule. You create the environment.

slides.heading: The Child's Job
slides.body: They decide WHETHER they eat and HOW MUCH. This is the hardest part to let go of. But when children control their own intake, they develop a healthier relationship with food long-term.

slides.heading: Why Forcing Backfires
slides.body: 'Just try one bite' actually increases food refusal over time. Pressure creates negative associations with food. Instead: serve the meal, eat together, model enjoyment, and trust your child's appetite signals.

activities.title: Feeding Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the principles behind stress-free toddler mealtimes.

cards.back: Satter's framework: YOU decide WHAT is served, WHEN meals happen, WHERE they eat. YOUR CHILD decides WHETHER to eat and HOW MUCH. Respecting this boundary removes mealtime power struggles.

'Just one more bite' and 'eat your vegetables' create negative associations with food and increase refusal over time. Pressure overrides hunger signals and can contribute to disordered eating long-term.

Fear of new foods is biologically normal in toddlers — it was an evolutionary protection against poisoning. It typically peaks between ages 2–3. Exposure, without pressure, is the evidence-based solution.
A child may need to see, touch, smell, and taste a new food 15–20 times before accepting it. Each exposure counts — even if they just look at it or touch it. Don't give up after a few rejections.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of toddler feeding before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of the Division of Responsibility and picky eating.

questions.question: According to the Division of Responsibility, who decides HOW MUCH the toddler eats?
options: The parent, to ensure adequate nutrition
The child, following their own hunger and fullness signals
A 50/50 negotiation between parent and child
The paediatrician, based on growth chart targets
questions.explanation: The Division of Responsibility (Ellyn Satter): the child decides whether to eat and how much. When parents try to control amounts, they override the child's internal hunger regulation, which can disrupt their natural relationship with food.

questions.question: How does pressure to eat ('just one more bite') affect toddlers long-term?
options: It teaches them to eat more variety over time
It has no significant effect on food acceptance
It actually increases food refusal and creates negative food associations
It only has negative effects if used at every meal
questions.explanation: Research consistently shows that pressure to eat (including bribing, forcing, and the 'one more bite' rule) increases food refusal over time by creating negative associations with mealtimes and overriding the child's internal regulation.

questions.question: How many exposures might a toddler need before accepting a new food?
options: 1–3 times
5–7 times
10–12 times
15–20 times
questions.explanation: Research shows toddlers may need 15–20 exposures to a new food before accepting it. Each exposure counts even if the child only looks at it, touches it, or smells it — without any pressure to eat it.

questions.question: What is 'food neophobia'?
options: A serious eating disorder requiring professional treatment
A biologically normal fear of new foods that peaks between ages 2–3
When a toddler stops eating a food they previously liked
An allergic reaction to novel foods
questions.explanation: Food neophobia (fear of new foods) is a biologically normal part of toddler development — an evolutionary protection against poisoning. It peaks around 2–3 years. The solution is repeated, pressure-free exposure.

content.prompt: Think about a recent stressful meal. Were you trying to control your child's eating (how much, what they ate)? How might the Division of Responsibility change that meal?

slides.heading: It Takes 15–20 Exposures
slides.body: Children may need to see, touch, smell, and taste a food 15–20 times before accepting it. Each exposure counts — even if they just touch it and put it aside. Don't give up after 3 tries.

slides.heading: The 'Safe Food' Strategy
slides.body: Always include at least ONE food you know they'll eat at every meal. This prevents the meal becoming a power struggle and ensures they won't go hungry while being exposed to new foods alongside their safe option.

slides.heading: Get Them Involved
slides.body: Children who help choose, shop for, and prepare food are significantly more likely to eat it. Even toddlers can wash vegetables, tear lettuce, stir ingredients. Ownership creates curiosity.

content.question: Your toddler refuses dinner and asks for a biscuit instead. Best approach?

options.label: 'No biscuit until you eat your vegetables'
Give them the biscuit to avoid conflict
'Dinner is what we're having now. Your tummy might be hungry later — that's okay.'
Make them something different they'll eat

content.explanation: This approach holds the boundary (dinner is dinner) without punishment or power struggles. If they choose not to eat, they learn that mealtimes are structured and that being hungry is a natural consequence — not a punishment.

activities.title: Transitions Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore the PREP transition framework, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How smoothly do transitions (leaving the park, bath time, bedtime) typically go in your house?

slides.heading: Step 1 — Prepare Ahead
slides.body: Before the transition happens, decide what you’ll say and when. Give warnings: ‘In 10 minutes, we’ll be leaving the park.’ Visual timers work brilliantly for toddlers who can’t grasp abstract time.

slides.heading: Step 2 — Preview What’s Next
slides.body: Walk through exactly what will happen, step by step. Be specific: ‘After we eat lunch, daddy will go to the shop and you’ll stay home with mummy. You and mummy will play together until I get back.’ The more details, the safer they feel.

slides.heading: Step 3 — Empower With Choice
slides.body: Give them a micro-job within the transition: ‘Would you like the blue towel or the grey towel for bath?’ ‘You can be our toy leader when we pack up!’ Choice = control = cooperation.

activities.title: Transition Framework Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand why transitions are hard and what helps.

cards.back: Toddlers live in the present moment and have no concept of future time. 'In 10 minutes' is meaningless to them. Abrupt transitions feel like things are being taken away without warning — which is genuinely distressing.

Give warnings before the transition happens: '10 minutes until we leave the park.' Use a visual timer so the countdown is concrete, not abstract. Toddlers respond much better to seeing time passing than hearing about it.

Walk through exactly what will happen, step by step: 'After lunch, daddy goes to the shop. You'll stay home with mummy. You and mummy will play until I get back.' Specifics create safety — the more detail, the less anxiety.

Give a micro-choice within the transition: 'Would you like the blue towel or the grey towel for bath?' Choice creates a sense of control, which dramatically reduces resistance. The choice must be real and within a boundary you set.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of the PREP transition framework.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of how to make transitions smoother for toddlers.

questions.question: Why are transitions particularly difficult for toddlers?
options: They are being deliberately defiant
They don't understand abstract time concepts and experience transitions as sudden losses
They haven't been taught how to behave in transition situations
They need more snacks to manage transitions better
questions.explanation: Toddlers live in the present moment and have no abstract concept of time. 'In 10 minutes' means nothing — abrupt transitions feel like something is being taken away without warning, which is genuinely distressing.

questions.question: What does the 'Prepare Ahead' step in PREP involve?
options: Setting out all the items needed for the next activity beforehand
Giving warnings before the transition happens and using visual timers
Discussing what happened during the previous activity
Making sure the child has eaten before any transition
questions.explanation: Prepare Ahead means giving time warnings ('10 minutes until we leave') and using a visual timer so the countdown is concrete. Visual timers work far better than verbal warnings because toddlers can see time passing.

questions.question: Why does giving a choice during a transition ('blue towel or grey towel?') help?
options: It distracts them from the transition itself
It gives them a sense of control, which reduces resistance
It teaches them decision-making skills for later life
It makes the transition take longer, giving them more time to adjust
questions.explanation: Choice creates a sense of control — and control is what toddlers most fear losing during transitions. A small, real choice within a boundary you set dramatically reduces resistance by shifting their attention from 'am I losing something?' to 'which option do I want?'

questions.question: What should the PREP 'Preview' step include?
options: A brief mention of what happens next
A very specific, step-by-step description of exactly what will happen
A list of rules for during the next activity
An explanation of why the transition is necessary
questions.explanation: The Preview step should be highly specific: walk through exactly what will happen, step by step. 'After lunch, daddy will go to the shop, you'll stay with mummy, you'll play together, then I'll be back.' Specifics create safety — the unknown is what creates anxiety.

content.prompt: Pick three transitions that regularly cause meltdowns in your household (e.g., leaving the park, bathtime, mealtimes). Write a PREP script for each one, including the specific warning, explanation, and choice you’ll offer.

slides.heading: Bedtime PREP
slides.body: ‘In 5 more minutes, we’ll say night night to our toys, put pyjamas on, brush teeth, read two books, snuggle and say night night. Would you like to listen to a song during snuggles or have quiet snuggles tonight?’

slides.heading: Car Seat PREP
slides.body: ‘You’re going to put one arm in, then the other. Then I’ll buckle in the middle. Can you show your toy puppy how car seats work? Puppy doesn’t know!’ Making them the ‘teacher’ gives them agency and distracts from resistance.

slides.heading: Playdate Ending PREP
slides.body: ‘In 15 minutes, your friend’s mummy will come to pick him up. We’ll gather up all his things and then say bye bye. Should we bring our dog out with us to wave goodbye?’ Involving them in the ‘closing ceremony’ helps them process the ending.

content.question: You need to leave for school in 10 minutes and your toddler is deep in play. What’s the best PREP approach?

options.label: Just pick them up and go when it’s time
Give a warning, explain what’s next, offer a choice about what to bring
Wait until they finish playing naturally
Bribe them with a treat to leave

content.explanation: PREP in action: ‘In 10 minutes, we’ll say bye to toys, get shoes on, and drive to school. Do you want to bring teddy or bunny in the car?’ Warn, explain, give a small choice.

activities.title: Redirection Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore the gentle redirect, check in with how you currently respond to unwanted behaviour.

content.question: When your toddler does something you don't want, how calm and consistent is your response?

slides.heading: Step 1 — Notice the Behaviour
slides.body: Narrate what you see without judgment: ‘I see you’re hitting the dog with your cup.’ This shows your child you’re paying attention and gives them a mirror for their actions.

slides.heading: Step 2 — Name & Guide
slides.body: Name what’s appropriate: ‘Cups are for drinking, and the dog likes it when you’re gentle with your hand.’ Then guide them to try again: ‘Let’s try that again gently.’ Show them what ‘gentle’ looks like with your hands.

slides.heading: Step 3 — Follow Through
slides.body: If the behaviour continues, calmly follow through: ‘I see you’re still hitting the dog with the cup. The cup is going away for now and we can try again to use it safely and gently later.’ No anger, no lectures. Just a natural outcome.

activities.title: Gentle Redirect Steps
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand each step of the gentle redirect approach.

cards.back: Narrate what you observe without judgment: 'I see you're hitting the dog with your cup.' Neutral narration shows the child you've noticed, gives them a mirror for their actions, and avoids shame-based language.

Name the rule and show the alternative: 'Cups are for drinking, and the dog likes it when you're gentle.' Then guide them to try again: 'Let's try gentle hands.' Show physically what 'gentle' looks like.

If the behaviour continues, calmly apply a natural outcome: 'I see you're still hitting with the cup. The cup is going away for now. We can try again later.' No anger, no lectures. Just a calm, related consequence.

Gentle redirect teaches without shaming. It addresses the BEHAVIOUR not the child ('cups are for drinking' vs 'you're being naughty'). Teaching happens when the child is calm — this keeps them calm enough to learn.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of the gentle redirect method.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of the Notice, Name, Guide, Follow Through approach.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Notice' step in the gentle redirect?
options: To warn the child that a punishment is coming
To narrate what you observe without judgment, giving the child a mirror for their actions
To explain why the behaviour is wrong
To get the child's attention before giving a timeout
questions.explanation: Noticing involves neutral narration: 'I see you're hitting the dog with your cup.' This shows the child you've seen the behaviour and gives them a chance to self-correct, without shame or judgment.

questions.question: What should the 'Guide' step include?
options: A clear explanation of the consequences if behaviour continues
Showing the alternative physically and verbally: 'Let's try gentle hands — like this'
A firm 'no' and removal from the situation immediately
Waiting to see if the child corrects themselves first
questions.explanation: The Guide step shows the child what TO do (not just what not to do): name the rule, describe the alternative, and physically demonstrate it. Toddlers learn through modelling, not just verbal instruction.

questions.question: What makes the Follow Through step effective?
options: Using a loud, firm voice so the child knows you mean it
Applying a calm, related consequence without anger or lengthy lectures
Repeating the rules again before any action is taken
Waiting until the end of the day to address the behaviour
questions.explanation: The Follow Through involves a calm, related consequence applied without anger: 'The cup is going away for now. We can try again later.' No anger or lectures — just a predictable, natural outcome that teaches cause and effect.

questions.question: Why is 'Cups are for drinking' better than 'You're being naughty'?
options: It's longer and therefore more effective as a correction
It addresses the behaviour without shaming the child's identity or character
It teaches vocabulary alongside the correction
It's easier for toddlers to remember
questions.explanation: Behaviour-focused language ('cups are for drinking') addresses the action without targeting the child's character. Shame-based language ('you're naughty') attacks identity and creates defensiveness, which prevents learning.

content.prompt: Think of 3 recurring behaviours that frustrate you. Write a gentle redirect script for each one (Notice what you see, Name the rule, Guide them to try again, Follow through if needed).

activities.title: Coping Skills Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore coping tools for your toddler, check in with your own toolkit.

content.question: How equipped do you feel to help your toddler manage big, overwhelming emotions?

slides.heading: Deep Breathing for Little Ones
slides.body:
Slow breathing releases GABA in the brain — a chemical that creates feelings of safety and relaxation. Make it fun:
• Bunny breath (quick sniffs)
• Smell the flower, blow the candle
• Lion breath (big roar exhale)
• Dragon breath
• Blow bubbles

Say: ‘When big feelings come, we can take a BIG breath to feel better.’

slides.heading: Physical Release
slides.body:
Help your child channel aggressive energy into something safe:
• Stomp feet like a dinosaur
• Jumping jacks
• Bounce a ball hard
• Tense and release: ‘Squeeze your whole body tight like a lemon... now let go!’

Say: ‘If we feel like hitting, first we can stomp our feet to let the anger out.’

slides.heading: When Can They Use These?
slides.body: Important: your child may not be able to access coping tools IN THE MOMENT until around age 4. But start introducing and practising them early, during calm moments. You’re wiring their brain to cope in the future. Think of it as depositing tools into their emotional bank account.

activities.title: Coping Skills Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand how toddlers can learn to manage big emotions.

cards.back: Coping skills must be practised during calm moments, not mid-meltdown. You're depositing tools into their emotional bank account. Most toddlers can't access these tools independently until around age 4, but planting seeds now matters.

Slow breathing releases GABA in the brain — a chemical that creates feelings of safety. Make it fun: 'Smell the flower, blow the candle', 'Bunny breath' (quick sniffs), 'Lion breath' (big roar exhale). Toddlers learn through play.

Aggressive energy needs a safe outlet. Teach: 'When we feel like hitting, we stomp like a dinosaur.' Jumping jacks, bouncing a ball hard, tense-and-release ('squeeze like a lemon, now let go!') — all safe physical outlets for big feelings.

Sensory input helps the nervous system regulate. Effective options: squishing playdough, smelling something pleasant, listening to birds or water, drinking water slowly. Nature walks are deeply restorative even for 2-year-olds.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of teaching coping skills to toddlers.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of how and when to teach coping tools.

questions.question: When is the best time to teach a toddler coping skills?
options: During a meltdown, while emotions are at their peak
During calm moments — not mid-crisis
Just before bedtime as a relaxation routine
After a meltdown as part of the review
questions.explanation: Coping skills must be practised during calm times. During a meltdown, the thinking brain is offline and the child cannot access new strategies. Teaching calmly builds the tools that become available when they're eventually needed.

questions.question: How does slow breathing help a toddler during big emotions?
options: It distracts them from what they're feeling
It releases GABA — a brain chemical that creates feelings of safety and calm
It only works for children over age 5 with practice
It's mainly useful for adults rather than toddlers
questions.explanation: Slow, deep breathing triggers the release of GABA in the brain — a neurotransmitter associated with calm and safety. It also activates the parasympathetic nervous system, helping the body come down from fight-or-flight.

questions.question: At approximately what age can toddlers start accessing coping tools independently during emotional moments?
options: 12–18 months
2 years
Around 4 years
6 years
questions.explanation: Most children can't independently access coping strategies in the heat of the moment until around age 4. But introducing and practising them earlier still matters — you're building the neural pathways and vocabulary that will be available when the child's brain matures.

questions.question: What is the purpose of physical release strategies like stomping or jumping?
options: To tire the child out so they fall asleep more easily
To give aggressive energy a safe physical outlet before it becomes hitting
To teach them that exercise solves emotional problems
To redirect their attention away from what upset them
questions.explanation: Physical release gives aggressive or overwhelming energy a safe outlet. 'When we feel like hitting, we stomp like a dinosaur' teaches that the impulse is understandable AND that there are body-safe ways to express it.

content.question: Which coping category do you think your toddler would respond to best?
options: Deep breathing (bunny breath, lion breath)
Physical release (stomping, jumping)
Creative release (angry chalk, feelings painting)
Sensory soothing (playdough, water, textures)

slides.heading: Creative Release
slides.body:
Show your toddler how to express feelings through art:
• Angry chalk: designate a special colour for when they’re upset
• Feelings painting or drawing
• Build something that represents the feeling with blocks
• Use animals and toys to act out the situation

From age 3, encourage them to tell the story of their emotions.

slides.heading: Sensory & Nature
slides.body:
Sensory input helps the body relax:
• Squish playdough or putty
• Smell something pleasant (flower, essential oil)
• Listen to birds or water
• Drink some water slowly

Nature walks are deeply restorative: take a ‘rainbow walk’ finding something red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

slides.heading: Helpful Words to Practise
slides.body:
Give them phrases to use instead of hitting, screaming, or shutting down:
• ‘I wasn’t done with that!’
• ‘Mummy/Daddy, I need help.’
• ‘I feel sad/mad.’
• ‘I didn’t like that.’
• ‘I need a hug.’
• ‘That wasn’t OK with me.’

Practise these in calm moments and celebrate when they use words instead of actions.

content.prompt: Design a personalised ‘calm-down kit’ for your child. What breathing technique will you practise? What physical release? What sensory item? What helpful phrases will you start teaching this week?

activities.title: Parent Emotion Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore managing your own emotions, take an honest check-in.

content.question: How well do you manage your own emotional reactions during your toddler's hardest moments?

slides.heading: Calm → Frustrated
slides.body:
CALM: Feeling light, open, rolling with the chaos. Strategy: accept feelings, hold boundaries, teach coping skills.

FRUSTRATED: Tension in arms and chest. ‘Ugh, just do what I say’ thoughts creeping in. Strategy: deep breaths, sip of water to reset.

slides.heading: Angry → Explosive
slides.body:
ANGRY: Breathing intensified, difficult to speak constructively. Strategy: take a breath, feel your feet on the ground, relax your shoulders.

EXPLOSIVE: Heart pounding, physically aggressive urges, dizzying rage. Strategy: STOP. Take a break. Leave the room if children are safe. Schedule self-care time.

slides.heading: The Repair Roadmap
slides.body:
When you’ve totally lost it (and you will — you’re human):
1. Stop. Walk away if safe.
2. Cool down (splash water on face, breathe).
3. Come back and repair: ‘I’m sorry I yelled. That wasn’t okay. I was feeling really frustrated and I didn’t handle it well. I love you.’

Repair teaches children that relationships can recover from ruptures.

activities.title: Parent Emotion Management Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand how to recognise and manage your own emotional escalation.

cards.back: Monitor your own stress in real time: Calm → Frustrated → Angry → Explosive. Each level has body signals and specific strategies. The goal is to intervene early (at Frustrated), before reaching Explosive.

At Frustrated: tension in arms and chest, impatient thoughts. At Angry: intensified breathing, difficulty speaking constructively. At Explosive: heart pounding, dizzying rage, physical urges. Your body always gives warning — learn to read it.

When you've escalated: (1) Say 'I need a moment.' (2) Physical reset — cold water on wrists, step outside, 10 deep breaths. (3) Self-talk: 'I'm a good parent having a hard moment.' (4) Return when your heart rate has slowed.

'I yelled and that wasn't okay. Even grown-ups have big feelings sometimes. I'm working on handling mine better. I love you.' Repair models that relationships recover from ruptures — one of the most important lessons you can teach.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of managing your own emotions as a parent.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of parental emotion regulation and repair.

questions.question: Why is managing your own emotions so critical during your toddler's meltdowns?
options: Because children learn emotion regulation from watching how their parents handle distress
Because children are more likely to listen to calm parents
Because it sets a good example for later in life
Because toddlers can sense when parents are stressed
questions.explanation: You cannot co-regulate your toddler if you're dysregulated yourself. Your calm nervous system is the tool that helps theirs settle. This is why parental self-regulation isn't just about you — it's the mechanism through which your child learns to regulate.

questions.question: What is the best action at the 'Frustrated' level of the emotion thermometer?
options: Push through and finish the interaction before resetting
Take a deep breath, sip water, or reset briefly before continuing
Tell your toddler you need a break and leave them alone
Only act when you reach the Angry level
questions.explanation: Intervening at the Frustrated level — before escalating further — is much easier than trying to recover from Angry or Explosive. Simple strategies like deep breaths, drinking water, or a brief pause can prevent further escalation.

questions.question: What does a repair after losing your cool look like?
options: Pretending it didn't happen so your child forgets
Apologising sincerely, naming what happened, and reconnecting with your child
Giving your child something nice to make up for it
Waiting until they bring it up to avoid dwelling on it
questions.explanation: Repair involves a sincere acknowledgment: 'I yelled and that wasn't okay. I was frustrated and I handled it badly. I love you.' This teaches children that mistakes are human, accountability matters, and relationships can heal — which is enormously valuable modelling.

questions.question: Why is occasional yelling NOT a sign of being a bad parent?
options: Because children benefit from seeing parents get angry
Because yelling is only harmful when it happens every day
Because what matters most is the pattern of repair and reconnection after losing your cool
Because all parents yell and it has no measurable effect
questions.explanation: Every parent loses their temper sometimes. What matters is what comes after: acknowledging the rupture, apologising, and reconnecting. Research shows that repair after rupture builds resilience in children and models healthy emotional recovery.

content.prompt: Fill in your own thermometer: What does your body feel like at each level (calm, frustrated, angry, explosive)? What specific strategies will you use at each stage to bring yourself back down?

slides.heading: The Stages of Losing It
slides.body:
GO — Cool, confident. You’re responding well.
SLOW DOWN — Tone rising, impatience creeping in.
PAUSE — Harsh tone, unkind words slipping out.
RESTART — You’ve snapped. Time to step back.
RED HOT — You’ve totally lost it. Body shaking, kids crying. Stop everything.

slides.heading: The Restart Protocol
slides.body:
At any ‘restart’ level:
1. Say: ‘I need a moment.’ Walk away (ensure children are safe).
2. Physical reset: cold water on wrists, step outside, 10 deep breaths.
3. Self-talk: ‘I’m a good parent having a hard moment.’
4. Return when your heart rate has slowed.

slides.heading: Repair, Don’t Shame-Spiral
slides.body:
Rather than beating yourself up, use these moments to model emotional recovery for your children:
‘I yelled and that wasn’t okay. Even grown-ups have big feelings sometimes. I’m working on handling mine better. I love you.’

This teaches them that mistakes don’t define us — repair does.

content.statement: Yelling at your toddler occasionally means you’re a bad parent.
content.explanation: Every parent loses their cool sometimes. What matters is what you do AFTER. Repair — acknowledging the rupture and reconnecting — actually builds resilience in your child and models healthy emotional processing.

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How consistent and predictable is your current daily routine for your toddler?

slides.heading: Why Routines Matter
slides.body: Toddlers thrive on knowing what comes next. A flexible routine — a ‘flow’ — lets them mentally prepare for transitions without the stress of rigid timing. We’re NOT aiming for minute-by-minute schedules that leave everyone stressed.

slides.heading: Morning Flow Example
slides.body:
Wake up → Go potty → Breakfast → Playtime (while you do dishes) → Brush hair → Get dressed → Leave for school/activities.

The ORDER stays consistent. The exact TIMES can flex based on the day.

slides.heading: Evening Flow Example
slides.body:
Dinner → Bath time → Pyjamas → Brush teeth → 2 books → Bed.

Keeping the same sequence every evening signals to their brain: ‘Sleep is coming.’ This reduces bedtime battles dramatically because there are no surprises.

activities.title: Building a Flexible Toddler Routine
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the key principles of creating flow in your toddler's day.

cards.back: Toddlers thrive on knowing what comes NEXT — not on exact clock times. A flexible 'flow' maintains consistent order without rigid timing. Wake up → breakfast → playtime → lunch → nap → outdoor time → dinner → bath → bed. The sequence is predictable; the exact times can flex.

Dinner → Bath → Pyjamas → Brush teeth → 2 books → Bed. The same sequence every evening signals to the toddler's brain: 'Sleep is coming.' This dramatically reduces bedtime battles because there are no surprises about what's happening next.
Toddlers struggle with abrupt transitions. Give 5-minute and 2-minute warnings: 'In 5 minutes, bath time.' This gives them time to mentally prepare and reduces resistance significantly.

Predictability gives toddlers a sense of control and safety in a world where adults make most decisions for them. When children know what comes next, their nervous system stays regulated — leading to better cooperation, fewer meltdowns, and easier transitions.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of building flexible toddler routines.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a toddler 'flow' and a rigid schedule?
options: A flow is less structured and unpredictable
A flow maintains consistent ORDER of activities while allowing times to flex
A schedule is better for toddlers
There is no meaningful difference
questions.explanation: A 'flow' maintains the same sequence of activities each day (giving toddlers predictability and security) without requiring exact clock times. This provides the structure toddlers need while allowing flexibility for real life.

questions.question: Why does a consistent evening routine reduce bedtime battles?
options: Because children are tired by evening
Because the same sequence signals to the toddler's brain that sleep is coming — no surprises
Because parents are more patient in the evening
Because it's darker in the evening
questions.explanation: A predictable bedtime sequence (bath → pyjamas → teeth → books → bed) trains the toddler's nervous system to begin winding down at each step. The ritual removes uncertainty — a common driver of bedtime resistance.

questions.question: Why do transition warnings ('In 5 minutes, bath time') help toddlers?
options: They give parents time to prepare
They distract toddlers
They give toddlers time to mentally prepare for the change, reducing resistance
They teach toddlers to tell time
questions.explanation: Toddlers struggle with abrupt transitions because they have limited control over their world. Warnings give psychological preparation time, making transitions feel less like interruptions and more like expected events.

questions.question: What matters MOST in a toddler's daily routine?
options: Everything happens at exactly the same time each day
The consistent ORDER of activities is maintained, even if times flex
The child gets plenty of unstructured free time
Following a professional consultant's exact schedule
questions.explanation: Toddlers gain security from knowing what comes NEXT, not from rigid clock times. Consistent sequencing provides the predictability they need without the stress of rigid schedules.

content.prompt: Map out your ideal morning and evening routine ‘flow’. What order works for your family? Where do the biggest friction points happen, and how could consistency help?

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How confident are you about knowing when and how to drop your toddler's nap?

slides.heading: Signs It’s Time
slides.body:
Usually between ages 3–5 (rarely at 2.5):
• Taking 20+ minutes to fall asleep at night
• Night wakings increasing
• Refusing 2+ naps per week consistently
• Early morning wake-ups

Don’t rush it! Try capping the nap first before dropping entirely.

slides.heading: Cap Before You Cut
slides.body:
Before eliminating naps, try reducing duration:
• Age 1–2.5: around 2 hours
• Age 2.5: reduce to 1–1.5 hours
• Age 3: maximum 1 hour

If capping doesn’t solve night-time issues, it may be time to transition to quiet rest time instead.

slides.heading: The Little-By-Little Sleep Plan
slides.body:
For bedtime battles and teaching independent sleep:
1. Place a chair next to their bed
2. Stay quiet and boring — no engaging, singing, or back rubs
3. Repeat your ‘boring script’: ‘I’m here, you’re safe. Close your eyes.’
4. Each night, move the chair slightly further toward the door
5. After ~2 weeks, you’re at the door, then outside

This builds self-soothing without abandonment.

activities.title: Dropping the Nap: What You Need to Know
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand when and how to transition away from napping.

cards.back: Usually between ages 3–5 (rarely at 2.5). Signs: taking 20+ minutes to fall asleep at night, night wakings increasing, refusing 2+ naps per week consistently, early morning wake-ups. Don't rush it — try capping the nap first before dropping entirely.

Before eliminating naps, reduce duration: Age 1–2.5: around 2 hours. Age 2.5: reduce to 1–1.5 hours. Age 3: maximum 1 hour. If capping doesn't solve night-time issues, transition to quiet rest time instead of a full nap.

When the nap ends, replace it with quiet rest time (30–60 mins): child stays in their room with books, puzzles, or soft toys. This maintains the rhythm of the day, gives parents a break, and helps the child avoid becoming overtired.

When dropping the nap, temporarily move bedtime EARLIER (30–60 mins) to compensate for lost sleep. Without this, overtiredness sets in by 3pm and both nap resistance and bedtime battles worsen. After 2–3 weeks, gradually shift bedtime back.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of the nap transition.

questions.question: At what age do most children typically drop their nap?
options: Age 1–2
Age 3–5
Age 6–7
questions.explanation: Most children naturally drop their nap between ages 3–5. Dropping before this (especially at age 2) is usually too early and can lead to overtiredness, worse behaviour, and increased night waking.

questions.question: What should you try BEFORE fully eliminating the nap?
options: Stopping the nap suddenly on one day
Capping the nap duration at a shorter length first
Moving nap time to later in the day
Eliminating the nap every other day
questions.explanation: Capping (reducing nap duration) is the recommended first step. It allows the child to gradually adjust to less daytime sleep without the abrupt change that full elimination creates. Many families cap for several weeks before fully transitioning.

questions.question: When a toddler drops their nap, what bedtime adjustment helps prevent overtiredness?
options: Move bedtime 1–2 hours later to tire them out more
Keep bedtime exactly the same as before
Move bedtime 30–60 minutes earlier temporarily
Skip bedtime routine on non-nap days
questions.explanation: Without the nap's restorative sleep, toddlers accumulate sleep pressure faster. Temporarily moving bedtime earlier (30–60 minutes) prevents overtiredness — which paradoxically makes toddlers harder to settle. After 2–3 weeks, gradually shift back.

questions.question: What is 'quiet rest time' and why is it used?
options: Forced nap time where the child must sleep
A designated period in the child's room with quiet activities — maintaining the rest rhythm without requiring sleep
Sitting still at the dinner table
TV time to wind down
questions.explanation: Quiet rest time (30–60 minutes with books, puzzles, or soft toys in their room) replaces the nap's structure without requiring sleep. It gives both child and parent a restorative break and helps prevent afternoon overtiredness during the transition period.

content.statement: Most children should stop napping by age 2.
content.explanation: Most children still benefit from naps until age 3–5. Dropping too early often leads to overtiredness and worse behaviour. Look for consistent signs over several weeks before making the change.

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How ready do you feel for your child's transition to kindergarten or school?

slides.heading: Focus on Independence, Not ABCs
slides.body:
It’s tempting to worry about counting and letters. But the skill that matters most is independence:
• Can they open their lunchbox?
• Can they ask when they need something?
• Can they use the toilet on their own?
• Can they put on shoes and jacket?

Practise these through play and low-pressure games.

slides.heading: PREP for Drop-Off
slides.body:
Use PREP to walk through every detail before the first day. Role-play school life with dolls. Read school-themed books together.

At drop-off: stay calm, stay confident. Your feelings are contagious! If you waver, they’ll worry something’s wrong.

Give a comfort anchor: a bracelet, a drawn heart on their hand, a note in their lunchbox.

slides.heading: Expect After-School Meltdowns
slides.body:
They’ve been keeping it together all day in a new environment. That’s exhausting! They’ll melt down at home because YOU are their safe person.

The meltdown won’t be about school — it’ll be about crayons or bananas. Look beneath the surface and validate: ‘You’re feeling really upset. Sometimes I feel upset too.’

activities.title: Kindergarten Readiness: What Really Matters
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand what actually prepares your child for their first school experience.

cards.back: The skills that matter most: Can they open their lunchbox? Can they ask when they need something? Can they use the toilet alone? Can they put on shoes and jacket? Academic knowledge matters far less than self-help independence in the first months of school.

Before the first day, walk through every detail: Preview (what school looks like), Remind (what to do if scared), Explain (what happens if they miss you), Practise (role-play school with toys). Read school-themed books. Familiarity reduces fear.

At drop-off: stay calm, stay confident. Your feelings are contagious! If you waver, they'll worry something's wrong. Give a comfort anchor — a bracelet, a drawn heart on their hand, a note in their lunchbox. Keep the goodbye ritual brief, warm, and certain.

They've kept it together all day in a new environment. They'll melt down at home because YOU are their safe person. The meltdown won't be about school — it'll be about crayons or bananas. Look beneath the surface: 'You're feeling really upset. Big days are exhausting.'

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of kindergarten readiness.

questions.question: What is the MOST important skill for kindergarten readiness?
options: Knowing the alphabet and counting to 20
Being able to write their name
Independence skills — using the toilet alone, opening lunchbox, asking for help
Being able to sit still for 30 minutes
questions.explanation: Independence skills matter far more than academic knowledge in the first months of school. A child who can manage their own body, belongings, and needs — and ask for help when needed — adjusts to school far more easily than a child who knows their ABCs but can't open their lunchbox.

questions.question: What does PREP stand for in preparing for school drop-off?
options: Prepare, Respond, Evaluate, Plan
Preview, Remind, Explain, Practise
Practice, Rest, Eat, Play
Prepare, Reassure, Encourage, Praise
questions.explanation: PREP (Preview what school looks like, Remind what to do if scared, Explain what happens if they miss you, Practise through role-play) reduces first-day fear by making the unknown familiar through preparation and rehearsal.

questions.question: Why should a parent's goodbye be brief and confident, not long and emotional?
options: Long goodbyes make teachers' jobs harder
Your emotional state is contagious — wavering signals to your child that there IS something to worry about
Short goodbyes save time
Children don't care how long goodbye takes
questions.explanation: Children read parent emotion as information about safety. A warm, confident, brief goodbye communicates: 'This is safe. I'll be back. You've got this.' An emotional, drawn-out goodbye communicates: 'I'm worried too — maybe you should be too.'

questions.question: Why do after-school meltdowns happen, and what should parents do?
options: They're a sign the child isn't ready for school yet
The child has been holding it together all day — they melt down at home because it's their safe space. Validate the emotion.
They're manipulating parents for attention
Parents should be firmer about the meltdown not being acceptable
questions.explanation: After-school meltdowns happen because children expend enormous effort regulating themselves in a new, unfamiliar environment all day. Home — and you — is where they feel safe enough to release. This is a healthy sign of a secure attachment, not a problem.

content.prompt: List 3 independence skills you can start practising with your child this week (opening containers, dressing themselves, asking for help). How will you make each one fun?

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How do you feel when your toddler hits, bites, or is physically aggressive? Are you able to stay calm?

slides.heading: Why They Hit/Bite
slides.body:
Toddlers hit and bite because:
• They can’t express feelings in words yet
• Their impulse control is undeveloped
• They’re testing cause-and-effect
• They’re overwhelmed

It’s NOT because they’re ‘mean’ or you’re a bad parent.

slides.heading: What to Do In the Moment
slides.body:
1. Block/stop the behaviour: ‘I won’t let you hit’
2. Check the other child first (this also teaches empathy)
3. Name the feeling: ‘You were angry’
4. Offer the alternative: ‘Hands are for gentle touch. You can stamp your feet when you’re angry’

Stay neutral — big reactions (positive OR negative) reinforce the behaviour.

slides.heading: When Another Child Hits Yours
slides.body:
This is hard! Model the response you’d want:
• Comfort your child first
• Don’t shame the other child
• ‘That hurt. We need to use gentle hands’
• Remove your child from the situation if needed
• Don’t force your child to ‘hit back’

activities.title: Hitting & Biting: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand why toddlers hit and what actually works.

cards.back: Toddlers hit and bite because: they can't express feelings in words yet, impulse control is undeveloped, they're testing cause-and-effect, or they're overwhelmed. It's NOT because they're 'mean' or you're a bad parent. It's a communication failure, not a character flaw.

1. BLOCK: 'I won't let you hit.' 2. CHECK the other child first (models empathy). 3. NAME the feeling: 'You were angry.' 4. OFFER the alternative: 'You can stamp your feet when you're angry.' Stay neutral — big reactions reinforce the behaviour.

Both shock/horror AND laughing reinforce hitting. Toddlers are cause-and-effect experimenters — a dramatic parental reaction is very interesting and motivating to repeat. Stay neutral, brief, and matter-of-fact. Less reaction = less repetition.

Saying 'don't hit' without an alternative leaves the toddler with the same overwhelming feeling and no acceptable outlet. Always pair the limit ('I won't let you hit') with an alternative ('you can squeeze this pillow / stamp your feet / use your words').

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of handling toddler hitting and biting.

questions.question: Why do toddlers hit and bite?
options: Because they are naturally aggressive
Because they can't express feelings in words and have undeveloped impulse control — it's communication, not cruelty
Because parents haven't set enough consequences
Because they watched it on TV
questions.explanation: Toddler physical aggression is almost always communication — expressing overwhelm, frustration, or excitement without the language to do so. Understanding this changes the parent's response from moral outrage to problem-solving.

questions.question: Why do dramatic reactions (shock, shouting) make hitting WORSE?
options: They upset the parent
Toddlers are cause-and-effect explorers — an interesting reaction is motivating to repeat
They confuse the toddler
They teach the toddler that hitting is funny
questions.explanation: Toddlers are experimenting with cause and effect. A dramatic, emotional parental reaction is highly interesting and motivating to repeat. A neutral, brief, matter-of-fact response removes the interesting consequence and reduces repetition.

questions.question: In the 4-step response to hitting, why do you check the other child FIRST?
options: Because the other child is more hurt
Because it models empathy and connects the toddler's action with its impact on others
Because parents need to assess the injury
Because the hitting child needs time alone
questions.explanation: Checking on the other child first models empathy in action — showing the toddler that their actions affect others. It also briefly removes the parental attention that sometimes reinforces hitting.

questions.question: What must you ALWAYS pair with 'I won't let you hit'?
options: A time-out
An explanation of why hitting is wrong
An alternative acceptable behaviour for expressing the same feeling
A consequence like losing a toy
questions.explanation: Teaching the alternative is essential. 'Don't hit' without a replacement leaves the toddler with the same overwhelming feeling and no acceptable outlet. Offering an alternative (stamping, squeezing, using words) builds emotional regulation skills.

content.prompt: Write a specific script you’ll use next time your toddler hits. Include what you’ll say to them AND what you’ll do with your body (get low, hold hands, etc.).

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How confident are you in handling sharing conflicts between toddlers without forcing them to share?

slides.heading: Forced Sharing Doesn’t Teach Sharing
slides.body: Imagine someone at work took your coffee and said ‘You need to share!’ You’d be furious. Forced sharing teaches that other people can take your things whenever they want. True generosity comes from choice, not force.

slides.heading: What to Do Instead
slides.body:
• Teach turn-taking: ‘When you’re finished, then it’s their turn’
• Use a timer for popular toys
• Protect their right to finish: ‘She’s still using that. You can have it when she’s done’
• Model generosity: ‘Would you like to share some of my snack?’
• Praise genuine sharing when it naturally occurs

activities.title: Sharing & Turn-Taking: What Actually Works
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand why forced sharing backfires and what to do instead.

cards.back: Imagine someone at work took your coffee and said 'You need to share!' Forced sharing teaches: other people can take your things whenever they want. True generosity comes from choice, not force — and choice doesn't develop until ages 3–4.

'When you're finished, then it's their turn.' Use a timer for popular toys. Protect their right to finish: 'She's still using that. You can have it when she's done.' This teaches: your turn will come — an important lesson in delayed gratification.

Sharing skills genuinely develop between ages 3–4. 43% of parents expect it before age 3 — when it's simply not developmentally possible. Praise genuine voluntary sharing ('I noticed you gave her a turn — that was really kind') to reinforce when it naturally occurs.

Offer your child a bit of your snack. Let them see you share with others. Say 'I'd like to share some of my...' around them. Children learn generosity by watching it demonstrated, not by being forced to perform it.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of sharing and turn-taking.

questions.question: Why doesn't forced sharing teach real generosity?
options: Children are naturally selfish
Forced sharing teaches 'others can take your things whenever they want' — the opposite of voluntary generosity
Children need to learn that sharing is required
Parents are not consistent enough
questions.explanation: True generosity is voluntary — it comes from wanting to give, not from having things taken. Forced sharing teaches children to be more protective of possessions, not less — and it doesn't develop the internal motivation that real generosity requires.

questions.question: At what age do sharing skills genuinely develop?
options: Age 1–2
Age 3–4
Age 5+
questions.explanation: Sharing skills develop between ages 3–4. Before this, the cognitive and emotional capacity for voluntary sharing simply isn't there. Understanding this prevents frustration from expecting behaviour a child cannot yet produce.

questions.question: What is the best approach when two toddlers want the same toy?
options: Take the toy away so neither child gets it
Give it to the younger/more upset child
Teach turn-taking: 'When you're finished, then it's their turn' — protecting each child's right to finish
Insist the child shares immediately
questions.explanation: Turn-taking respects each child's rights while teaching delayed gratification — a crucial skill. 'When you're done, then it's their turn' communicates: you will get your turn, and your turn will come to an end too.

questions.question: How do children best learn to be genuinely generous?
options: Through consistent forced sharing
By being rewarded for sharing
By watching adults model generosity voluntarily in everyday life
By being told sharing is important
questions.explanation: Children learn generosity through observation — watching adults voluntarily share, offer, and give. Modelling 'I'd like to share some of my...' creates an internal template for generosity that children naturally replicate over time.

content.scenario: Your child is having a full meltdown in the supermarket because you said no to a toy. Other shoppers are staring. What do you do?

options.label: Get down to their level and validate: 'You really wanted that toy. It's hard when we can't have something we want.'
options.outcome: Validating the emotion doesn't mean giving in. Your child feels heard, and the intensity often drops. You can then offer a choice: 'Would you like to help me pick the apples or the bananas?'

options.label: Firmly say 'Stop it — you're embarrassing yourself' and keep walking
options.outcome: Shaming during a meltdown escalates it. Your child can't access rational thinking during emotional flooding. They need co-regulation first, boundaries second.

options.label: Give in and buy the toy to stop the scene
options.outcome: This teaches: meltdowns = getting what I want. Short-term peace, long-term pattern. The next meltdown will be bigger.

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?

content.question: When your toddler has a major meltdown, how calm are YOU able to stay?

slides.heading: B — Be Clear Ahead of Time
slides.body:
Before a tantrum even starts, set your child up for success. Use PREP to explain what’s happening, what’s expected, and what comes next. When children know the plan, they feel safer and tantrums reduce dramatically.

R — Release Your Reaction When It Begins
When the tantrum starts, YOUR first job is to regulate yourself. Take a breath. Drop your shoulders. Unclench your jaw. Your child is a sponge for your energy — if you escalate, they will too.

slides.heading: E — Eye Level & A — Allow the Feels
slides.body:
Get down to their level physically. This is powerful body language that says ‘I’m here, I’m safe, I’m not a threat.’ Keep your voice low and calm.

Allow the feelings to flow without trying to fix, distract, or shut them down. Tantrums aren’t the time to teach — they’re the time to CONNECT. ‘You’re really upset right now. I’m right here.’

slides.heading: T.H.E. — Tell, Highlight, Echo
slides.body:
T — Tell Them Where the Bumpers Are: Once calming, set the boundary: ‘It’s not okay to throw things. I’ll keep you safe.’

H — Highlight a Yes: Redirect to what they CAN do: ‘You can’t throw the blocks, but you CAN stomp your feet!’

E — Echo the Same Thing Over and Over: Repeat your calm phrase like a broken record. Repetition is soothing and helps their overwhelmed brain process.

activities.title: The BREATHE Method: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to master each step of the BREATHE tantrum navigation system.

cards.back: B — BE CLEAR AHEAD OF TIME: Use PREP to set expectations before situations that trigger tantrums. R — RELEASE YOUR REACTION: When it starts, regulate YOURSELF first. Take a breath, drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw. Your child is a sponge for your energy — if you escalate, they will too.

E — EYE LEVEL: Get down to their physical level — powerful body language that says 'I'm here, I'm safe, I'm not a threat.' A — ALLOW THE FEELS: Let feelings flow without fixing, distracting, or shutting them down. 'You're really upset right now. I'm right here.'

T — TELL THEM THE BOUNDARIES: Once calming begins, set the limit: 'It's not okay to throw things. I'll keep you safe.' H — HIGHLIGHT A YES: Redirect to what they CAN do: 'You can't throw the blocks, but you CAN stomp your feet!'

E — ECHO THE SAME THING OVER AND OVER: Repeat your calm phrase like a broken record. 'I know you're upset. I'm here. I know you're upset. I'm here.' Repetition is soothing and helps an overwhelmed brain process. Don't change the script — consistency is the medicine.

activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of the BREATHE method.

questions.question: In the BREATHE method, what does the FIRST step 'B' stand for?
options: Breathe in, breathe out
Be clear ahead of time — use PREP to set expectations before triggering situations
Be calm no matter what
Block the behaviour immediately
questions.explanation: B stands for 'Be Clear Ahead of Time.' Many tantrums are preventable when children know what's coming. Using PREP before transitions, unfamiliar situations, or places with temptations significantly reduces meltdown frequency.

questions.question: Why is getting to the child's eye level (the 'E' step) so powerful?
options: It helps parents see the situation from the child's perspective
It signals 'I'm here, I'm safe, I'm not a threat' through body language — physical positioning communicates safety
It prevents the child from running away
It makes it easier to talk quietly
questions.explanation: Physical positioning communicates before words. Getting to eye level — rather than looming over a distressed child — signals in a primal, body-level way: 'I am with you, I am safe, I am not threatening you.' This helps the child's nervous system begin to settle.

questions.question: During 'A — Allow the Feels,' what should you NOT do?
options: Stay physically nearby
Say 'I'm right here'
Try to fix, distract, or shut down the emotion
Use a calm voice
questions.explanation: The 'Allow' step means letting the emotional storm pass without interference — no fixing, no distracting, no 'calm down.' Tantrums are not the time for teaching — they're the time for CONNECTION. The child cannot access the learning brain while emotionally flooded.

questions.question: Why does the 'E — Echo' step recommend repeating the same phrase over and over?
options: Because children don't listen the first time
Repetition of a calm phrase is soothing and helps the overwhelmed brain process — consistency is the medicine
To show parents are in control
To prevent the child from talking back
questions.explanation: The overwhelmed toddler brain cannot process new information. A consistent, calm repeated phrase — 'I know you're upset, I'm here' — acts as a soothing anchor. The sameness itself is regulating, like a familiar song.

content.prompt: Write your personal BREATHE script for a common tantrum scenario in your house. What will you say at each step? What does your ‘broken record’ phrase sound like?

content.question: How accurate do you think your expectations are for what your toddler can actually do at their age?

slides.heading: Impulse Control & Limits
slides.body:
Age 1–2: Can’t consistently understand ‘forbidden’ or manage impulses. This is NORMAL.
Age 3: Understands rules only SOME of the time.
Age 4: Can manage impulses MORE of the time.

56% of parents have inaccurate expectations here. 36% believe children under 2 have self-control. They simply don’t yet.

slides.heading: Sharing & Turn-Taking

Age 4: More capable, but still needs practice.

Sharing skills genuinely develop between ages 3–4. 43% of parents inaccurately expect it before age 3.

slides.heading: Tantrums & Sitting Still
slides.body:
Tantrums are normal from age 1. Self-control develops around 3.5–4 and takes years to be consistent.

Sitting still:
• Age 1: Can’t expect it

Have food plated and ready BEFORE asking your toddler to sit.

Tantrums are normal from age 1. Self-control begins developing around 3.5–4 and takes years to be consistent. A 2-year-old having tantrums is not misbehaving — their brain literally cannot regulate big emotions yet. This is biology, not defiance.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of realistic toddler expectations.

questions.question: At what age does consistent sharing ability typically begin to develop?
options: Age 1–2
Age 3–4
Age 5+
questions.explanation: Sharing skills genuinely begin developing between ages 3–4. Before this, the cognitive and emotional capacity for voluntary, consistent sharing simply isn't present. 43% of parents expect sharing before age 3, which creates unnecessary conflict.

questions.question: How long can a typical 2-year-old realistically sit still?
options: 10 minutes
5 minutes
1–3 minutes
30 seconds
questions.explanation: A 2-year-old can realistically sit still for only 1–3 minutes. Having food ready before asking them to sit, and not expecting extended table time, prevents unnecessary conflict based on a capability they don't yet have.

questions.question: A 2-year-old who cannot consistently understand 'no, don't touch that' is:
options: Deliberately defiant and needs firmer consequences
Developmentally normal — impulse control is still being built
Behind in development
Being manipulative
questions.explanation: At ages 1–2, the prefrontal cortex — the brain's impulse control centre — is in very early development. Children literally cannot consistently resist impulses yet. Understanding this reduces frustration and prevents ineffective or harsh responses to normal developmental behaviour.

questions.question: Tantrums are considered developmentally normal until approximately what age?
options: 18 months
2 years
3.5–4 years (when self-control begins consistently developing)
5–6 years
questions.explanation: Tantrums are a normal expression of emotional overwhelm when self-regulation skills are still developing. Self-control begins to reliably emerge around 3.5–4 years old, but even then it requires years of practice and support.

content.statement: A typical 2-year-old should be able to sit still at the dinner table for 10 minutes.
content.explanation: A 2-year-old can realistically sit for only 1–3 minutes. Having overly high expectations leads to unnecessary power struggles.

content.question: How confident are you in understanding the typical developmental milestones for your toddler's age?

slides.heading: By Age 1
slides.body:
Cognitive: Connects objects to names, knows things exist even if hidden.
Social: Develops toy preferences, enjoys peekaboo, separation anxiety starts.
Communication: Understands some words, responds to name, says simple words.
Physical: Walking alone or with support, pincer grasp, tosses balls.

slides.heading: By Age 2
slides.body:
Cognitive: Explores new places, experiments to solve problems, sorts by colour.
Social: Imitates social behaviour, says ‘No’, tantrums emerge with big emotions.
Communication: Up to 50 words, sentences up to 4 words.
Physical: Walks stairs with rail, uses spoon/fork, ready for potty training (20–30 months).

slides.heading: By Age 3–4
slides.body:
Age 3: Learns names easily, enjoys independence, anticipates routines, beginning to share, speaks in sentences, dresses self, advanced climbing.

Age 4: Understands time and size concepts, engages in cooperative play, can resolve some conflicts, tells detailed stories, hops and balances, draws recognisable shapes.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of toddler developmental milestones.

questions.question: When does separation anxiety typically first develop?
options: At birth
Around age 1
Age 2
Age 3
questions.explanation: Separation anxiety typically begins around age 1 — when babies first understand that people exist even when not visible (object permanence). This is a healthy developmental milestone, not a problem to be solved, though it can be managed with warm, consistent drop-off routines.

questions.question: What communication milestone is typical by age 2?
options: Full sentences of 10+ words
Up to 50 words and sentences of up to 4 words
Reading simple words
Only a few single words
questions.explanation: By age 2, most children have approximately 50 words and can produce short 2–4 word sentences. Language development varies widely — some children have more, some fewer words. If concerned, a speech pathology referral is appropriate.

questions.question: When are most children developmentally ready for potty training?
options: Age 12–18 months
Age 18–20 months
Age 20–30 months
Age 3–4 years
questions.explanation: Most children show potty training readiness between 20–30 months. Some children are earlier, some later. Forcing training before physical and cognitive readiness typically increases resistance and accidents — readiness, not age, should guide timing.

questions.question: What does a 4-year-old's cooperative play indicate developmentally?
options: That they're ahead of schedule
That they understand their role in relation to others and can work toward shared goals — a significant cognitive and social leap
That they prefer group activities
That they're ready for school
questions.explanation: Cooperative play (working with others toward a shared goal — 'let's build a house together') requires understanding of others' intentions and roles. This replaces parallel play (playing beside others) and is a major social-cognitive developmental achievement.

content.question: How confident are you that your child's caregivers (daycare, nanny, grandparents) are consistent with your approach at home?

slides.heading: You Don’t Need to Be There 24/7
slides.body: These strategies work for every family setup — stay-at-home, working, single parents. The magic happens when you’re consistent in YOUR home. Your child will flourish inside and outside your home when you provide that predictable, safe foundation.

slides.heading: If They’re in Daycare/School
slides.body:
• Choose a daycare that aligns with your parenting approach
• Be consistent at home — both parents and caregivers using the same strategies
• Release the worry about what happens when they’re not with you

When home is consistent, that’s MORE than enough.

slides.heading: If They Have a Nanny or Grandparent
slides.body:
• Share these strategies with your caregiver
• Discuss approaches daily so you’re on the same page
• Focus on your home being the anchor of consistency

The most important thing: all caregivers in your home using the same language, the same boundaries, the same warmth.

activities.title: Childcare & Consistency: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand how to make these strategies work across all care environments.

cards.back: These strategies work for every family setup — stay-at-home, working, single parents. The magic happens when YOU are consistent in YOUR home. Children adapt to different environments — and flourish everywhere — when home provides a predictable, warm, safe foundation.

Choose daycare that broadly aligns with your approach. Be consistent at home — both parents using the same strategies. Release worry about what happens when they're not with you. When home is consistent, that's more than enough. Children are resilient adapters in different environments.

Share these strategies with your caregiver. Discuss approaches daily so you're on the same page. Focus on your home being the anchor of consistency. Most important: all caregivers in your home using the same language, the same boundaries, the same warmth.

The most powerful consistency is YOUR relationship with your child. A secure, loving, predictable parent-child attachment is the foundation everything else is built on. Even if other caregivers do things differently, your child knows who their safe base is — and that's enough.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of maintaining consistency across childcare environments.

questions.question: What is the most important factor for toddler wellbeing when families use multiple caregivers?
options: All caregivers doing exactly the same things
Children being in daycare as little as possible
Consistent warmth, language, and boundaries within the HOME environment
Parents monitoring all caregiver interactions closely
questions.explanation: Children adapt to different environments naturally — daycare, grandparents, and home will all be different. What matters most is that home provides a consistent, predictable, warm base. This gives the child a secure foundation from which to navigate all other environments.

questions.question: If you discover the daycare does things differently from your approach at home, you should:
options: Remove your child immediately
Try to change everything at daycare to match your home
Maintain consistency in your own home — children adapt to different contexts
Feel guilty that you're not consistent enough
questions.explanation: Children are natural context-adapters. They learn 'at home we do it this way, at daycare we do it that way' — just as adults behave differently in different contexts. Consistency at home is the most powerful variable you control.

questions.question: When sharing strategies with a nanny or grandparent caregiver, the focus should be on:
options: Giving them a detailed manual of rules to follow exactly
The language, warmth, and boundaries that create safety — not perfection in method
Making sure they do things identically to you
Monitoring their interactions to ensure compliance
questions.explanation: Sharing the spirit of your approach (consistent warmth, the same key phrases, the same core boundaries) is more important than identical execution. Grandparents and nannies bring their own relationships with your child — align on the essentials, not every detail.

questions.question: What is the most powerful consistency in your child's life?
options: Perfect routine management across all environments
All caregivers using identical methods
Your loving, predictable, secure relationship with your child
The daycare environment and approach
questions.explanation: The parent-child attachment relationship is the most powerful factor in a child's development and wellbeing. A secure, loving, consistent relationship with you is the foundation that makes everything else work — even in the presence of inevitable inconsistencies across different care environments.

content.prompt: Who are the caregivers in your child’s life? List them and note one thing you could share with each person to help create consistency across environments.

activities.title: Resilience Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore resilience, take a moment to reflect on where your child is right now.

content.question: How resilient do you feel your child is when they face setbacks or challenges?

slides.heading: Resilience ≠ Toughness
slides.body: Resilience isn't about suppressing emotions or 'hardening up'. It's the ability to feel difficult feelings, navigate setbacks, and bounce back with support. The foundation? A secure relationship with at least one trusted adult.

slides.heading: The 3 Pillars
slides.body:
1. CONNECTION: 'I have people who love me'
2. CAPABILITY: 'I can handle hard things'
3. CONTRIBUTION: 'I matter and can make a difference'

Every interaction with your child either builds or undermines these pillars.

slides.heading: Let Them Struggle (A Little)
slides.body: The urge to rescue is strong, but children learn resilience through manageable challenges — not through having every obstacle removed. Ask yourself: 'Is this a situation where they need my help, or where they need my belief in them?'

activities.title: Resilience Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand what actually builds resilience in children.

cards.back: Resilience is NOT suppressing emotions or 'hardening up.' It's the ability to feel difficult feelings, navigate setbacks, and bounce back — usually with support. It's built through relationship, not hardship.

Connection: 'I have people who love me.' Capability: 'I can handle hard things.' Contribution: 'I matter and can make a difference.' Every interaction with your child either builds or erodes these three pillars.

Children build resilience through manageable challenges — not through having every obstacle removed. The coaching question: 'Is this a situation where they need my help, or where they need my belief in them?'

Process praise ('You worked really hard') builds internal motivation. Trait praise ('You're so smart') creates fragility — because if they fail, it means they're not smart. The simple word YET transforms 'I can't' into 'I can't yet.'

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of resilience and growth mindset.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of what builds genuine resilience in children.

questions.question: What is resilience in children?
options: The ability to suppress emotions and push through without complaining
The ability to feel difficult feelings, navigate setbacks, and bounce back — usually with support
Having a personality that is naturally unaffected by hard experiences
Never needing parental help to solve problems
questions.explanation: Resilience is not toughness or emotional suppression — it's the capacity to feel hard things AND recover. It's built through relationships, not hardship alone. A secure connection is its foundation.

questions.question: What are the three pillars of resilience?
options: Intelligence, obedience, and self-sufficiency
Connection, capability, and contribution
Persistence, courage, and independence
Love, boundaries, and routine
questions.explanation: The three pillars are: Connection ('I have people who love me'), Capability ('I can handle hard things'), and Contribution ('I matter and can make a difference'). Every parenting interaction either builds or erodes these.

questions.question: How does trait praise ('You're so smart!') affect resilience?
options: It builds confidence that lasts into adulthood
It creates fragility — when they fail, it threatens their entire identity
It has no significant effect either way
It only becomes problematic in teenagers, not younger children
questions.explanation: Trait praise ('You're so smart') creates fragility because it ties worth to a fixed quality. When the child fails, they think 'If I'm smart and I failed, maybe I'm not smart.' Process praise ('You worked really hard') builds motivation that's resilient to setbacks.

questions.question: What is the coaching question that distinguishes over-helping from appropriate support?
options: 'Do they need me to do this for them?'
'Will they ask for help if they need it?'
'Is this a situation where they need my help, or where they need my belief in them?'
'Am I being a good parent by stepping back?'
questions.explanation: The coaching question — 'Do they need my help or my belief in them?' — helps distinguish genuine need (step in) from productive struggle (step back and express confidence). Both are forms of support; choosing correctly is the skill.

content.prompt: Think about a recent time your child faced a challenge. Did you step in to solve it, or support them in solving it themselves? What would the 'coaching approach' have looked like?

slides.heading: Praise the Process
slides.body: Instead of 'You're so smart!' try 'You worked really hard on that!' Process praise builds internal motivation. Trait praise creates fragility ('If I'm smart, what does it mean when I fail?').

slides.heading: Normalise Failure
slides.body: Share your own mistakes: 'I messed up at work today. Here's what I learned.' Let them see you struggle and persist. Model the self-talk: 'This is hard. I'm going to try a different approach.'

slides.heading: The YET Poster
slides.body:
Make a family 'YET wall'. When someone says 'I can't do this', add 'yet' and put it on the wall:
• 'I can't ride a bike... yet'
• 'I can't do long division... yet'
• 'I can't make friends at my new school... yet'

Revisit it monthly to celebrate progress.

content.question: Your child says 'I'm terrible at maths, I'll never get it.' Best response?

options.label: 'No you're not — you got an A last year!'
'Maths is really hard for you right now. What part is tricky? Let's figure it out.'
'Maybe maths just isn't your thing — focus on what you're good at'
'You just need to practice more — try harder'

content.explanation: Acknowledging the struggle validates their feeling while 'right now' implies it's temporary. Asking what's tricky shows belief they CAN work through it with support.

activities.title: Bullying Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore bullying, take a moment to reflect on your current situation.

content.question: How confident do you feel recognising the signs that your child might be experiencing bullying?

slides.heading: Behavioural Red Flags
slides.body:
• Reluctance to go to school (stomach aches, headaches)
• Coming home hungry (lunch stolen or afraid to eat alone)
• Withdrawal from friends or activities they used to enjoy
• Unexplained marks, torn clothing, missing belongings
• Mood changes: irritability, sadness, anger
• Sleep disruption, bed-wetting in older children
• Decline in schoolwork

slides.heading: Digital Bullying Signs
slides.body:
• Anxiety around their phone/device
• Deleting messages or hiding screens
• Refusing to go online (or obsessively checking)
• Emotional after being online
• New accounts or changed passwords
• Withdrawal from family life

slides.heading: How to Open the Conversation
slides.body:
Don't ask 'Are you being bullied?' (they'll say no). Instead:
• 'What was the worst part of your day?'
• 'If I asked your best friend how you're going, what would they say?'
• 'Is there anyone at school who's not very kind?'
• 'What's lunchtime like? Who do you hang out with?'

activities.title: Recognising Bullying Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the key signs and distinctions around bullying.

cards.back: Bullying is repeated, targeted, and involves a power imbalance. A one-off mean comment is unkind but not bullying. Both need addressing — but the response differs. Understand which you're dealing with before acting.

Watch for: reluctance to go to school, coming home hungry (lunch being stolen), unexplained marks, torn clothing, missing belongings, sleep disruption, and declining schoolwork. Children often don't disclose — their behaviour speaks first.

Signs of cyberbullying: anxiety around their device, deleting messages or hiding screens, emotional reactions after being online, new accounts or changed passwords, and withdrawal from family life after screen use.

Don't ask 'Are you being bullied?' (they'll say no). Instead: 'What was the worst part of your day?' or 'Is there anyone at school who's not very kind?' Indirect questions open more doors than direct ones.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of recognising and responding to bullying.
