content.intro: Let's check your knowledge of how to identify bullying and open conversations about it.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines bullying (as opposed to general unkindness)?
options: Any mean comment made by one child to another
Repeated, targeted behaviour involving a power imbalance
Disagreements between children of the same age
Any physical contact that causes upset
questions.explanation: Bullying is defined by three elements: it's repeated, targeted at a specific individual, and involves a power imbalance. A one-off unkind comment is hurtful but not bullying — both need addressing but require different responses.

questions.question: Why might a child who is being bullied come home hungry at lunchtime?
options: They forgot to eat because they were playing
Their lunch is being stolen or they are afraid to eat in public areas
They don't like the school canteen food
They are too anxious about afternoon classes to eat
questions.explanation: Coming home hungry can be a sign that a child is having their lunch stolen, or is too afraid or isolated at lunchtime to eat in front of others. This is a commonly overlooked indicator worth asking about.

questions.question: Why is asking 'Are you being bullied?' usually ineffective?
options: Children don't know what bullying means at this age
It's too direct and children almost always answer no, even when something is happening
It introduces the idea of bullying when the child hasn't experienced it
It makes children feel weak for not handling it themselves
questions.explanation: Children rarely self-identify as 'being bullied' and will typically say no even when something is happening. Indirect questions ('What was the worst part of your day?', 'Is there anyone who isn't very kind?') open more honest conversations.

questions.question: What is the best FIRST response when your child discloses bullying?
options: Call the school immediately to report it
Tell them to stand up for themselves and fight back
Listen and validate without immediately jumping to fix it
Reassure them it will stop soon and they'll be fine
questions.explanation: The most important first step is listening without fixing: 'Thank you for telling me. That sounds really hard. I'm glad you trust me with this.' Children need to feel heard before they can receive help — jumping straight to action feels dismissive.

content.prompt: Answer honestly: How much do you know about your child's social world at school? Who are their friends? Who do they avoid? What happens at lunchtime?

slides.heading: First: Listen Without Fixing
slides.body: Your child needs to feel heard before they can accept help. Don't immediately call the school or tell them to 'just ignore it' (this minimises their pain). Say: 'Thank you for telling me. That sounds really hard. I'm glad you trust me with this.'

slides.heading: Teach Assertiveness (Not Aggression)
slides.body:
Practice scripts they can use:
• 'Stop. I don't like that.'
• Walk away with confidence (head up, shoulders back)
• Find a buddy — bullies target kids who are alone
• 'That's your opinion' (for verbal bullying)

Role-play these at home until they feel natural.

slides.heading: Working With the School
slides.body:
Document everything (dates, what happened, who witnessed).
Request a meeting with the teacher AND pastoral care.
Ask: 'What is the school's specific plan to address this?'
Follow up in writing.
If nothing changes, escalate to the principal.
Keep your child informed: 'I spoke to the school. Here's what's happening.'

content.question: Your child tells you a classmate is calling them names every day. What's your first response?

options.label: 'That must really hurt. Tell me more about what's been happening.'

content.explanation: Always listen first. 'Just ignore it' dismisses their pain. Calling the school immediately takes away their agency. Retaliating escalates. First validate, then strategise together.

activities.title: Anxiety Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore childhood anxiety, take a moment to check in.

content.question: How well do you feel you understand what anxiety looks like in your child?

options.label: I'm not sure what I'm seeing
I have a good handle on it

slides.heading: The Smoke Detector Analogy
slides.body: Everyone has a 'smoke detector' in their brain (the amygdala). In anxious children, this alarm is too sensitive — it goes off when there's no real danger, like when toast burns and sets off the fire alarm. The alarm isn't broken — it's just set too sensitive. Our job is to help recalibrate it.

slides.heading: Anxiety vs Normal Worry
slides.body:
ALL children worry sometimes. Anxiety becomes a concern when it:
• Stops them doing things they want to do
• Causes regular physical symptoms
• Lasts weeks/months, not days
• Is disproportionate to the situation
• Impacts school, friendships, or family life

slides.heading: The Accommodation Trap
slides.body: The most natural parenting instinct — removing the thing causing anxiety — actually makes anxiety WORSE long-term. When we let them avoid scary things, we confirm their brain's message: 'This IS dangerous.' Gradual, supported exposure is the evidence-based alternative.

slides.heading: The Worry Cycle (Goff)
slides.body: Sissy Goff identifies a predictable worry cycle in girls especially: trigger → anxious thought → physical sensation → avoidance → temporary relief → increased sensitivity. Each time we allow avoidance, the cycle gets shorter and the anxiety trigger list grows. Breaking the cycle means helping your child sit WITH discomfort rather than flee from it.

activities.title: Anxiety Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the key ideas behind childhood anxiety.

cards.back: The amygdala is the brain's 'smoke detector.' In anxious children it's over-sensitive — going off when there's no real danger, like toast smoke triggering a fire alarm. The alarm isn't broken, just over-calibrated. Our job is to help recalibrate.

All children worry sometimes. Anxiety becomes a concern when it stops them doing things they want to do, causes physical symptoms, lasts weeks rather than days, and is disproportionate to the situation.

The most natural instinct — removing what causes anxiety — actually makes anxiety worse long-term. Avoidance confirms the brain's message: 'This IS dangerous.' Gradual, supported exposure is the evidence-based approach.

A graduated list of 8–10 steps from least to most anxiety-provoking, tackled one at a time. Example for school anxiety: 1) Talk about school at home, 2) Drive past, 3) Walk to the gate, 4) Go inside for 10 minutes... Each rung proves: 'I survived this.'

content.statement: The best way to help an anxious child is to remove the source of their anxiety.
content.explanation: While it feels kind, accommodation (removing the scary thing) reinforces the anxiety loop. Gradual exposure — facing the fear in small, supported steps — is how the brain learns 'I can handle this.'

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of childhood anxiety before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of anxiety in children and teens.

questions.question: What is the amygdala's role in anxiety?
options: It controls logical thinking and helps children make good decisions
It is the brain's alarm system — in anxious children it fires too readily, even without real danger
It regulates sleep cycles which are disrupted by anxiety
It produces cortisol, the stress hormone
questions.explanation: The amygdala acts as the brain's smoke detector. In anxious children, it's over-sensitive — triggering an alarm response when there is no real danger. This is biology, not character weakness.

questions.question: When does normal worry become problematic anxiety?
options: As soon as the child worries about anything at all
When worry stops them from doing things they want to do, is disproportionate, and lasts weeks rather than days
When the child cries about the worry
When the parent notices they are worrying
questions.explanation: All children worry sometimes — it's a normal part of development. Anxiety becomes a clinical concern when it significantly impairs functioning: stopping enjoyable activities, causing physical symptoms, or lasting disproportionately long.

questions.question: Why does removing the source of a child's anxiety ('accommodation') often backfire?
options: It teaches children they can manipulate parents with anxiety
It doesn't give the child practice at managing discomfort on their own
It confirms the brain's message that the thing is genuinely dangerous, making the anxiety worse
It only backfires with older children, not young ones
questions.explanation: Accommodation sends the message: 'You're right to be afraid.' The brain interprets avoidance as evidence of real danger — increasing sensitivity. Gradual, supported exposure teaches the brain: 'I survived this. It was manageable.'

questions.question: What is a 'bravery ladder' in anxiety treatment?
options: A chart that rewards brave behaviour with prizes
A graduated series of steps from least to most anxiety-provoking, tackled one at a time
A metaphor for how tall and strong the anxious child can grow
A list of all the child's fears ranked from worst to best
questions.explanation: A bravery ladder is a graduated exposure plan: 8–10 steps from least to most scary, tackled sequentially. Each completed step gives the brain proof that 'I can handle this' — reducing anxiety about the next step.

slides.heading: Name It to Tame It
slides.body: Give the anxiety a name and character. 'Oh, Worry Monster is visiting again. What's he saying today?' This externalises the anxiety — your child isn't anxious, the Worry Monster is bothering them. This creates distance and a sense of control.

slides.heading: The Worry Window
slides.body: Designate a 15-minute 'worry time' each day. When anxious thoughts arise, they write them on a note and put them in a 'worry box' to discuss at worry time. Most worries feel smaller by then. This teaches them they can postpone worry — it doesn't have to consume their whole day.

slides.heading: The 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding
slides.body:
For acute anxiety moments:
• 5 things you can SEE
• 4 things you can TOUCH
• 3 things you can HEAR
• 2 things you can SMELL
• 1 thing you can TASTE

This brings them out of their head and into the present moment.

slides.heading: Bravery Ladders (Goff)
slides.body: Sissy Goff recommends building graduated 'bravery ladders' — a list of 8–10 steps from least to most anxiety-provoking, tackled one at a time. Example for school anxiety: 1) Talk about school at home, 2) Drive past school, 3) Walk to the gate, 4) Go in for 10 minutes… Each rung proves to the brain: 'I survived that. I can handle the next step.'

slides.heading: The Parental Anxiety Transfer
slides.body: Goff emphasises that anxious parents often unconsciously transmit their own worry to children. Your facial expressions, tone, and hovering teach your child the world isn't safe. Practice: before reacting, take one breath and ask yourself 'Is this MY anxiety or theirs?' Model calm confidence even when you feel anxious inside.

content.prompt: Which of these strategies would work best for your child? How will you introduce it? Write down a specific plan for this week.

slides.heading: The Gender Gap
slides.body: Girls are diagnosed with anxiety disorders at roughly double the rate of boys. Sissy Goff identifies several contributors: socialisation toward people-pleasing, perfectionism culture, social media comparison, relational aggression, and earlier puberty flooding the brain with hormones before coping skills are mature.

slides.heading: The Perfectionism Trap
slides.body: Many anxious girls aren't 'problem' children — they're TOO good. They over-prepare, over-achieve, and over-control because failure feels catastrophic. Signs: spending hours on homework that should take 30 minutes, refusing to submit 'imperfect' work, meltdowns over small mistakes, avoiding new activities where they might not excel immediately.

slides.heading: Building Brave, Not Fearless
slides.body:
The goal isn't to eliminate fear — it's to teach her to act DESPITE fear. Goff's approach:
• Normalise imperfection: share YOUR mistakes openly
• Praise process over outcome: 'I loved how you kept trying'
• Create safe failure zones: cooking, crafts, sport — where mistakes are expected
• Limit reassurance: instead of 'you'll be fine,' try 'you can handle hard things'
• Resist rescuing: let her struggle, sit with discomfort, find her own solutions

slides.heading: Connection Before Correction
slides.body: When your daughter is spiralling, she needs connection before strategy. Sit with her. Don't fix. Say: 'I'm here. You're safe. We'll figure this out together.' Once her nervous system calms (5–15 minutes), THEN introduce coping tools. A dysregulated child cannot learn — they can only feel.

content.question: Your 10-year-old daughter refuses to go to her friend's birthday party because 'what if no one talks to me?' Best approach?

options.label: 'Don't be silly, of course they will!'
'That worry sounds really real. Let's make a bravery plan together — what's one small step?'
'I'll come with you and stay the whole time'

content.explanation: Validating the feeling while building a graduated plan teaches her she can face fear. Dismissing ('don't be silly') invalidates. Allowing avoidance strengthens the anxiety. Staying the whole time accommodates rather than builds independence.

activities.title: Screen Time Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore screen time boundaries, take an honest look at where things stand.

content.question: How confident are you that screen time in your household is well-managed and balanced?

slides.heading: Age-Based Framework
slides.body:
Under 2: Minimal/no screens (video calls okay)
2–5: Max 1 hour/day of quality content
6–12: Clear limits — focus on balance with physical activity, sleep, homework
13+: Collaborative agreements — involve them in setting boundaries

Quality matters more than quantity. Interactive > passive.

slides.heading: The Family Media Agreement
slides.body:
Create together (not imposed):
• Screen-free zones (bedrooms, dinner table)
• Screen-free times (1 hour before bed, morning routine)
• What content is/isn't okay
• Consequences for breaking agreements
• Regular review dates

Display it where everyone can see — this applies to PARENTS too.

slides.heading: Signs of Problematic Use
slides.body:
Watch for:
• Irritability/meltdowns when screens are taken away
• Sneaking screen time
• Neglecting friends, activities, homework
• Sleep disruption
• Declining interest in non-screen activities
• Using screens to manage emotions exclusively

activities.title: Screen Time Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the principles behind healthy digital boundaries.

cards.back: The quality of screen content matters as much as time spent. Interactive content (video calls, creative apps) is far better than passive consumption. Fast-paced, stimulating content is harder on developing brains than slower, educational material.

Screen rules work best when created collaboratively, not imposed. Include: screen-free zones, screen-free times, what content is okay, and consequences for breaking the agreement. Display it visibly — and apply it to parents too.

Warning signs: irritability when screens are taken away, sneaking screen time, neglecting friends and activities, sleep disruption, declining interest in non-screen activities, using screens exclusively to manage emotions.

Social media and games are deliberately engineered to be addictive through variable rewards (like slot machines). Knowing this doesn't make children immune, but it helps them understand their own reactions — 'the app is designed to make me want more.'

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of healthy screen time boundaries.

content.intro: Let's check your knowledge of age-appropriate screen guidelines and warning signs.

questions.question: According to the AAP, what is the maximum recommended screen time per day for children aged 2–5?
options: 30 minutes
1 hour
2 hours
No limit if content is educational
questions.explanation: The AAP recommends maximum 1 hour per day of high-quality programming for ages 2–5. For children under 2, screen time should be avoided except for video calls with family.

questions.question: Which is a sign of problematic screen use in children?
options: Choosing to watch a favourite show after homework
Preferring screen time to some other activities
Irritability, sneaking screen time, and declining interest in all non-screen activities
Asking for extra screen time on weekends
questions.explanation: Problematic screen use includes: significant irritability when screens are removed, deliberately sneaking screen time, declining interest in previously enjoyed non-screen activities, sleep disruption, and using screens as the only emotional regulation strategy.

questions.question: Why is it important for parents to follow the Family Media Agreement too?
options: To show that rules apply equally to everyone and model the behaviour you want to see
Because children notice and will only comply if parents do too
Because parental screen use is the primary cause of children's screen dependency
Rules don't need to apply to parents — only children need limits
questions.explanation: Children notice parental hypocrisy immediately. A Family Media Agreement that applies to everyone — including parents — is both fairer and significantly more effective. Modelling the behaviour you want to see is the most powerful teaching tool.

questions.question: What makes interactive screen content better than passive consumption for developing brains?
options: It is always more educational than passive content
It requires active engagement and responses, more closely mimicking real-world learning
Interactive content has fewer advertisements
It's less likely to contain inappropriate material
questions.explanation: Interactive content (video calls, creative tools) requires active responses and engagement, which activates more learning processes in the brain. Passive consumption is more closely associated with reduced attention span and increased anxiety.

content.prompt: What are the current screen time rules in your house? Are they working? Draft a Family Media Agreement with input from your child(ren).

activities.title: Teen Communication Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore the teenage brain, check in with how communication is going.

content.question: How connected do you currently feel to your teenager?

slides.heading: The Brain Renovation
slides.body: The teenage brain is undergoing the biggest remodel since toddlerhood. The emotional centre (amygdala) is fully active, but the rational centre (prefrontal cortex) won't be complete until their mid-twenties. They're driving a car with a powerful accelerator and underdeveloped brakes.

slides.heading: Why They're So Emotional
slides.body: Puberty floods the brain with hormones that amplify emotions. Everything feels more intense — happiness, sadness, embarrassment, anger. They're not being dramatic — they genuinely FEEL things more strongly than you do. Saying 'calm down' is as useful as telling someone to stop hiccupping.

slides.heading: Risk-Taking Is Biological
slides.body: The reward centre of the teenage brain is hypersensitive, especially around peers. This is why they do things that seem stupid — the brain's reward signal (dopamine hit) literally drowns out the risk assessment. This is especially true in groups.

slides.heading: The Plasticity Window (Jensen)
slides.body: Frances Jensen's research reveals the teenage brain is MORE plastic than the adult brain — meaning it learns faster but is also more vulnerable. Every experience literally wires the brain. This is why addiction takes hold faster in teens, why trauma impacts more deeply, and why positive experiences and skill-building during this window have outsized lifelong effects.

slides.heading: Sleep & the Teenage Brain (Jensen)
slides.body: Jensen demonstrates that the teenage circadian clock genuinely shifts — melatonin release moves 1–2 hours later. They're biologically wired to fall asleep later and wake later. Early school start times work AGAINST their biology. Chronic sleep deprivation in teens impairs memory consolidation, emotional regulation, and impulse control — making every other problem worse.

activities.title: Teenage Brain Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand what's actually happening in your teenager's developing brain.

cards.back: The teenage brain is undergoing the biggest remodel since toddlerhood. The emotional centre (amygdala) is fully active, but the rational prefrontal cortex won't be complete until mid-twenties. They're driving with a powerful accelerator and underdeveloped brakes.

Puberty hormones amplify emotional intensity. Everything feels more intense — happiness, sadness, embarrassment, anger. Saying 'calm down' is as useful as telling someone to stop hiccupping. This is real biology, not drama.

The teenage brain's reward centre fires MORE intensely in the presence of peers than alone. Brain scans confirm this. Risk-taking around friends is biological — the dopamine hit literally drowns out risk assessment signals.

The same plasticity that makes the teenage brain vulnerable also makes it exceptionally responsive to positive experiences. Music, sport, creativity, deep friendships — all wire the brain more powerfully during adolescence than at any other time.

content.question: Why do teenagers take more risks when they're with friends?

options.label: Their brain's reward system is amplified by peer presence

content.explanation: Brain scans show the reward centres of teenage brains literally fire more intensely in the presence of peers. It's not attitude — it's neuroscience.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of the teenage brain before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of adolescent brain development and how it affects behaviour.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the teenage amygdala and prefrontal cortex at this stage?
options: Both are fully developed and functioning equally
The amygdala (emotional) is fully active, but the prefrontal cortex (rational) is still developing
The prefrontal cortex develops before the amygdala in teenagers
Neither is fully functional until adulthood
questions.explanation: The amygdala (emotional brain) is fully active during adolescence, while the prefrontal cortex (rational decision-making, impulse control) isn't complete until the mid-twenties. This mismatch is why teenagers feel intensely but don't always reason well under pressure.

questions.question: Why do teenagers genuinely FEEL things more intensely than adults?
options: They are less experienced at managing their emotions
Puberty hormones amplify emotional intensity in the brain
They choose to be dramatic to get attention
They have more time to dwell on their feelings
questions.explanation: Puberty floods the brain with hormones that genuinely amplify emotional intensity. It's not an act — teenagers experience emotions more intensely than adults do. Understanding this prevents dismissiveness and supports better responses.

questions.question: Frances Jensen's research shows that alcohol and cannabis affect the teenage brain:
options: Less severely than adult brains because teens are more resilient
In the same way as adult brains
More severely than adult brains because key structures are still developing
Only if used regularly, not occasionally
questions.explanation: Jensen's brain imaging research shows substances affect the developing teenage brain significantly more than adult brains. THC locks onto receptors in structures that are still being built. 'Experiments' during adolescence can cause permanent structural changes.

questions.question: What does 'positive plasticity' mean for parents of teenagers?
options: Teenagers are flexible and recover quickly from bad parenting
Positive experiences have STRONGER effects on the teenage brain than at any other life stage
Teenagers can unlearn bad habits more easily than adults
The teenage brain returns to normal after any temporary setbacks
questions.explanation: The same plasticity that makes the teenage brain vulnerable to harm also makes it exceptionally responsive to positive experiences. Investments in music, sport, deep friendships, and skill-building have disproportionately large and lasting effects during adolescence.

slides.heading: Talk Side by Side
slides.body:
Teenagers often talk more when you're NOT face to face. The best conversations happen:
• In the car
• While cooking together
• On a walk
• At bedtime (they'll suddenly want to talk at 10pm)

Don't force 'sit down and talk' sessions — create conditions for spontaneous connection.

slides.heading: Listen Without Fixing
slides.body:
Your teenager doesn't want you to solve their problems (even when the solution is obvious). They want to feel heard. Try:
• 'Tell me more about that'
• 'That sounds really hard'
• 'What do YOU think you should do?'
• 'I'm here if you want to talk more'

Advice that isn't asked for is rarely received well.

slides.heading: Choose Your Battles
slides.body:
Ask yourself: 'Will this matter in 5 years?'

Worth fighting for: Safety, respect, values, education
Not worth fighting for: Messy room, hair colour, clothing choices, music taste

Every battle costs relationship capital. Spend it on what truly matters.

content.prompt: When was the last time you had a meaningful conversation with your teen? What conditions were present? How can you create more of those conditions this week?

slides.heading: Substances Hit Harder (Jensen)
slides.body: Jensen's brain imaging studies show that alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine affect the teenage brain MORE severely than the adult brain. THC locks onto receptors in the hippocampus (memory) and prefrontal cortex (judgment) that are still being built. One heavy drinking episode can damage white matter connections that took years to develop. The brain doesn't fully recover — these aren't 'experiments,' they're permanent alterations.

slides.heading: Stress Wires the Brain for Anxiety
slides.body: Chronic stress during adolescence (academic pressure, social drama, family conflict) literally wires the stress response system to be hyperactive. Jensen calls this 'stress kindling' — repeated stress lowers the threshold for future stress responses. A teen under chronic pressure doesn't just feel stressed NOW — they're building a brain that's more anxiety-prone for life.

slides.heading: Digital Overload & Attention
slides.body: Jensen warns that constant digital switching (texts, apps, videos, notifications) is training the teenage brain for distraction, not focus. The brain strengthens whatever neural pathways are used most. A brain trained on 15-second videos builds weaker sustained-attention circuits. This isn't about willpower — it's structural.

slides.heading: The Good News: Positive Plasticity
slides.body: The same plasticity that makes the teenage brain vulnerable also makes it exceptionally responsive to positive experiences. Music lessons, sport, creative pursuits, deep friendships, meditation — all wire the brain in beneficial ways MORE powerfully during adolescence than at any other time. Invest in enrichment, not just protection.

content.statement: A teenager's brain recovers from a heavy drinking episode just as well as an adult's brain.
content.explanation: Jensen's research shows the opposite — the teenage brain is MORE vulnerable to alcohol damage because key structures are still developing. White matter damage from binge drinking during adolescence can have lasting effects on memory and cognitive function.

activities.title: Identity & Peer Pressure Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore identity and peer pressure, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How confident do you feel that your child knows who they are when peer pressure hits?

slides.heading: The Values Conversation
slides.body: Children who know their family's values have an anchor when peer pressure hits. But values must be DISCUSSED, not just assumed. Try: 'In our family, we value kindness, honesty, and showing up for each other. What values are important to YOU?'

slides.heading: Rehearsing 'No'
slides.body:
Role-play peer pressure scenarios BEFORE they happen:
• 'Everyone's doing it — come on!'
• 'You're such a baby if you don't'
• 'No one will know'

Practice responses: 'Nah, I'm good', 'I'll pass', 'My parents will literally kill me' (giving them a way out that saves face).

slides.heading: The Code Word
slides.body: Agree on a code word or text your child can send when they need rescuing from a situation without losing face. 'I’m going to text you PIZZA and you call me and say I have to come home.' No questions asked in the moment — debrief later.

activities.title: Identity and Peer Pressure Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the key ideas behind building a strong identity.

cards.back: Children who know their family's values have an anchor when peer pressure hits. But values must be discussed, not assumed. 'In our family, we value kindness and honesty. What values are important to YOU?' — the conversation itself builds the anchor.

Role-playing refusal scripts BEFORE they're needed: 'Nah, I'm good.' 'My parents literally drug test me.' 'I've got training tomorrow.' Practise until responses feel natural and automatic — not something they have to think up on the spot.

A pre-agreed code word or text your child can send when they need rescuing without losing face. You come immediately, no questions asked in the car. Debrief the next day. This simple system has saved many teenagers from unsafe situations.

Children who know who they are don't need others' approval to feel okay. Identity formation is the central task of adolescence. Your job: provide enough values-discussion that they have something solid to return to when pressure mounts.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of identity development and peer pressure strategies.

content.intro: Let's check your knowledge of how to build a strong sense of identity and prepare children for peer pressure.

questions.question: Why do children need to know their family's values BEFORE facing peer pressure?
options: So they can explain their decisions to their peers
Values provide an anchor — a solid identity to return to when pressure mounts
So they feel guilty if they make bad choices
So parents can hold them accountable later
questions.explanation: Values are an anchor — a stable identity that doesn't shift based on who is present. A child who knows what they stand for can say 'that's not who I am' under pressure, rather than needing to invent a reason in the moment.

questions.question: Why is it important to role-play exit scripts before peer pressure situations arise?
options: So children can memorise the perfect thing to say
Because practised responses feel natural and don't require thinking on the spot under pressure
To build confidence in general social situations
So parents know their children have been taught what to say
questions.explanation: Under social pressure, the thinking brain works less effectively. Having a practised, automatic response ('Nah, I'm good') removes the need to think of something when stress and peer influence are at their peak — making refusal much more likely.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the code word system?
options: A secret language for parents and children to communicate privately
An agreed text or word the child sends when they need rescuing without losing face with peers
A system for grading how well the child handled peer pressure
A way for parents to check in without being obvious
questions.explanation: The code word allows a child to signal they need help without the social cost of being seen to 'call mum.' They send a pre-agreed text, parent picks them up with no questions asked in the car, and they debrief calmly the next day.

questions.question: At what age is discussing family values explicitly with children most impactful?
options: Only in the teenage years, once peer pressure becomes real
Only in early childhood before peer pressure begins
Throughout childhood — the conversations build on each other over time
Values are absorbed automatically and don't need to be discussed
questions.explanation: Value conversations build on each other over time — starting in childhood with simple concepts ('we tell the truth even when it's hard') and becoming more nuanced as children grow. They're most effective when woven naturally into everyday conversation rather than delivered as lectures.

content.prompt: List your top 5 family values. Have you ever explicitly discussed these with your children? How could you bring these into a natural conversation this week?

lessons.title: A Friend Says They Don’t Want to Play

activities.title: Social Situations Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore common social situations for ages 5–8, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How confident do you feel coaching your child through social challenges at school?

slides.heading: Why It Happens
slides.body: At this age, friendships are fluid. A child who is your kid’s best friend on Monday may ignore them on Tuesday. This is developmentally NORMAL — they’re learning how relationships work. But it still hurts.

slides.heading: What to Say to Your Child
slides.body:
• ‘That must have felt really sad. It’s okay to feel that way.’
• ‘Sometimes friends need space. It doesn’t mean they don’t like you.’
• ‘What could you do next time? Maybe ask someone else to play, or find something fun to do on your own.’
• ‘You are a great friend. Not everyone will see that every day, and that’s okay.’

slides.heading: Build the Skill
slides.body:
Practice ‘friendship flexibility’ at home:
• Role-play: ‘If Sarah says no, what’s your Plan B?’
• Encourage multiple friendships — not just one best friend
• Teach: ‘You can’t control what others do, only how you respond’
• Read books about friendship disappointments together

activities.title: Social Coaching Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand how to coach children through common social challenges.

cards.back: Before coaching, validate: 'That must have felt really sad. It's okay to feel that way.' A child who feels heard is open to guidance. A child who feels dismissed goes underground — they stop sharing.

Friendships are fluid at this age. A best friend on Monday may ignore them on Tuesday. This is developmentally normal — they're learning how relationships work. Help your child build multiple friendships rather than depending on one.

Teach specific approach strategies: 'Can I play too?' (direct and simple). 'I've got a ball — want to play?' (offering something). 'Hey, want to play with me?' (to another solo child). Scripts practised at home are used at school.

In sibling conflicts, narrate without judging: 'I see two kids who both want the same toy.' This teaches THEM to problem-solve rather than relying on you as judge. Your job: teach skills, not referee every battle.

content.question: Your 6-year-old comes home crying because their friend said ‘I don’t want to be your friend anymore.’ Best response?

options.label: ‘That really hurt, didn’t it? Tell me what happened.’

content.explanation: Validate the emotion first. Dismissing (‘they didn’t mean it’) teaches them their feelings don’t matter. Jumping to fix it removes their agency. Listen, validate, then coach.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of coaching children through social situations.

content.intro: Let's check your knowledge of how to support children aged 5–8 through social challenges.

questions.question: When your child comes home upset about a social situation, what is the most important first step?
options: Call the other parent to resolve the issue
Tell them it's not a big deal and they'll be fine
Validate the emotion before offering any coaching or solutions
Ask the teacher to intervene at school
questions.explanation: Validation must come first. A child who feels heard is open to coaching. If you jump straight to fixing, your child learns their feelings don't matter — and eventually stops sharing. Listen, validate, then coach.

questions.question: Why is it important for children to have multiple friendships rather than one 'best friend'?
options: Having many friends shows better social development
It means they are less vulnerable when any single friendship hits a rough patch
Multiple friendships prevent bullying
One intense friendship is never healthy for children
questions.explanation: Children who have only one key friendship are emotionally vulnerable when that friendship hits difficulties. Multiple connections provide resilience — if one friendship is rocky, they have others to fall back on.

questions.question: What is the 'sportscaster approach' to sibling conflict?
options: Keeping score of who started conflicts to determine consequences
Narrating what you observe without judging, then asking them to problem-solve
Cheering for the child who is in the right
Removing yourself from the conflict entirely and letting them sort it out
questions.explanation: The sportscaster narrates: 'I see two kids who both want the same toy.' No judgment, no taking sides. Then: 'What's a solution that works for both of you?' This teaches conflict resolution skills rather than relying on parental adjudication.

questions.question: When is it appropriate for parents to intervene in a child's social conflict?
options: Immediately, to show the child you are on their side
Only for safety issues or sustained bullying — coach them to handle typical social conflicts themselves
Never — children should always solve their own problems
After the child has tried once and failed
questions.explanation: Parent intervention is a last resort for typical social conflicts in this age group. Coaching the child to handle it themselves builds the social competence they need. Reserve direct intervention for safety issues or sustained bullying.

slides.heading: What’s Happening
slides.body: Exclusion at lunch/recess is one of the most painful experiences for young children. They may not tell you directly — look for signs: coming home starving (didn’t eat), not wanting to go to school, saying ‘no one likes me.’

slides.heading: Scripts for Your Child
slides.body:
Teach approach strategies:
• Walk up and say: ‘Can I play too?’ (direct and simple)
• Offer something: ‘I’ve got a ball — want to play?’
• Find the other solo kid: ‘Hey, want to play with me?’
• If groups say no: ‘That’s okay, I’ll find something else’ (and walk away with head up)

slides.heading: Behind the Scenes
slides.body: Talk to the teacher — ask about buddy systems or structured play. Arrange playdates with one or two children to build connections outside school. Don’t over-manage, but do set up conditions for success.

content.prompt: Does your child have at least one solid friendship at school? If not, what’s one step you could take this week to help them build a connection (e.g. invite a classmate over)?

lessons.title: Someone Is Being Mean to Them

slides.heading: Mean vs Bullying
slides.body: Not all unkindness is bullying. Children at this age are still learning empathy and impulse control. A one-off mean comment is different from repeated, targeted harassment. Both need addressing, but the approach differs.

slides.heading: Teach the ‘So What’ Shield
slides.body:
For verbal meanness, practice responses that deflate the power:
• ‘So?’ (said calmly, then walk away)
• ‘Okay’ (shrug and turn to someone else)
• ‘That’s your opinion’ (then move on)

The goal: remove the reaction the mean child is looking for. Practice until it feels natural.

slides.heading: When Your Child IS the Mean One
slides.body:
This happens too. If you get the call from school:
• Don’t shame: ‘What happened? Tell me the whole story.’
• Build empathy: ‘How do you think Liam felt when you said that?’
• Repair: ‘What could you do to make this right?’
• Investigate: ‘Is something bothering you that made you act that way?’

content.scenario: Your 7-year-old comes home and says 'Ella told me I'm weird and nobody likes me.' They're visibly upset.

options.label: 'That must have really hurt. Tell me what happened.'
options.outcome: Validating first opens the door. Once they feel heard, you can coach: 'What do you think you could say next time?' This builds their own problem-solving skills.

options.label: 'Just ignore her — she's probably jealous'
options.outcome: Dismissing minimises their pain. They learn not to come to you with problems. The hurt doesn't go away just because you've labelled it as jealousy.

options.label: 'I'm calling Ella's mum right now'
options.outcome: Jumping to fix it removes your child's agency. For non-bullying situations, coach them first. Save parent intervention for serious or repeated issues.

slides.heading: Prepare, Don’t Protect
slides.body:
Anxiety about new things is normal. Your job isn’t to remove the anxiety but to help them walk INTO it:
• Visit the school/venue beforehand if possible
• Read social stories about what to expect
• Role-play: ‘Let’s practise what you’ll say when you walk in’
• Give a comfort object (small toy in pocket, bracelet)

slides.heading: The Brave Ladder
slides.body:
Break scary things into small steps:
1. Talk about the new thing at home
2. Drive past the school/building
3. Visit for 10 minutes
4. Stay for a short session
5. Full attendance

Celebrate each step. ‘You did something brave today.’

slides.heading: Morning Drop-Off Struggles
slides.body:
Keep goodbyes SHORT and confident:
• ‘I love you. You’re going to have a great day. I’ll be here at 3.’
• Don’t sneak away (breaks trust)
• Don’t linger (prolongs the agony)
• Create a goodbye ritual (special handshake, three kisses)
• Trust the teacher — most kids calm down within 5 minutes

content.instruction: Put these steps in order from least to most brave for a child starting at a new school:
items: Talk about the school at home
Visit for 10 minutes with a parent
Stay for a short trial session
correctOrder: Talk about the school at home
Drive past the school building
Visit for 10 minutes with a parent
Stay for a short trial session
Full first day attendance

slides.heading: Why Kids Lie
slides.body:
At 5–8, children lie for predictable reasons:
• To avoid punishment (‘I didn’t break it’)
• Wishful thinking (‘I have a pony at home’)
• To please you (‘Yes I brushed my teeth’)
• To test boundaries

Lying is actually a cognitive milestone — it requires understanding that other people have different knowledge. But it still needs addressing.

slides.heading: Don’t Set Traps
slides.body:
If you SAW them eat the cookie, don’t ask ‘Did you eat a cookie?’ You’re setting them up to lie. Instead: ‘I see you ate a cookie. We agreed to ask first. Next time, please ask.’

When they DO tell the truth about something hard: ‘Thank you for being honest. That was brave. Let’s figure this out together.’ Make honesty SAFE.

slides.heading: Build a Truth-Telling Culture
slides.body:
• Share YOUR mistakes: ‘I messed up today — here’s what happened’
• Reduce punishment for honesty: ‘Because you told me the truth, we’ll work this out together’
• Praise truth-telling more than you punish lying
• Avoid: ‘Are you LYING to me?’ (threatening) — try: ‘Let’s try that again. What really happened?’

content.title: Setting Traps vs Building Honesty

columnA.label: Don't Do This
items: 'Did you eat a cookie?' (when you saw them)
Punish honesty the same as lying

columnB.label: Do This Instead
items: 'I see you ate a cookie. We ask first.'
'Let's try that again. What really happened?'
Create safety: 'You can tell me anything'

content.reflection: Which column sounds more like your home right now?

slides.heading: It’s Normal (But Exhausting)
slides.body: Siblings aged 5–8 fight an average of 3–7 times per HOUR. It’s developmentally normal — they’re practising conflict resolution in the safest environment possible. Your job: teach skills, not referee every battle.

slides.heading: The Sportscaster Approach
slides.body:
Instead of judging who’s right, narrate what you see:
• ‘I see two kids who both want the same toy.’
• ‘It sounds like you’re both feeling frustrated.’
• ‘What’s a solution that works for both of you?’

This teaches THEM to solve conflicts rather than relying on you as judge.

slides.heading: Never Compare
slides.body:
The fastest way to destroy sibling relationships:
✘ ‘Why can’t you be more like your sister?’
✘ ‘Your brother never does this’
✘ Praising one in front of the other

✔ Instead: celebrate each child’s unique strengths separately
✔ Create one-on-one time with each child
✔ ‘You two will figure this out’ (show belief in their ability)

content.question: Your two kids are fighting over a toy. Both are screaming 'IT'S MINE!' What's the sportscaster approach?

options.label: 'Give it to your sister — she had it first!'
'I see two kids who both want the same toy. What's a solution that works for both of you?'
Take the toy away from both of them
'Stop fighting or you're both going to your rooms!'

content.explanation: The sportscaster narrates without judging. This teaches THEM to problem-solve rather than relying on you as the referee.

slides.heading: When They Ask About Death
slides.body:
‘Where do people go when they die?’

Be honest and age-appropriate: ‘When someone dies, their body stops working. Different families believe different things about what happens next. What’s important is that the people we love stay in our hearts and memories.’

Don’t say: ‘They went to sleep’ (creates fear of sleep) or ‘They went away’ (creates abandonment fear).

slides.heading: When They Ask About Divorce/Separation
slides.body:
‘Why don’t you and Daddy live together?’

‘Mum and Dad realised we’re better parents when we live in different houses. We both love you MORE than anything. Nothing about this is your fault. You’ll always have both of us.’

Reassure: their routine, their stuff, access to both parents. Answer questions honestly but simply.

slides.heading: Use Little Minds for Metaphors
slides.body:
When your child asks a question you don’t have the words for — about death, grief, fairness, bodies, or the world — try the Little Minds Big Questions tool. It creates gentle, age-appropriate metaphor-based stories that help children understand complex topics.

Visit: littleminds.mindcast.co.nz

content.prompt: What’s the hardest question your child has ever asked you? How did you handle it? Looking back, is there anything you’d do differently?

activities.title: Tween Years Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore tween situations, take a moment to check in.

content.question: How well do you feel you understand what your tween (aged 9–12) is navigating socially?

slides.heading: The Group Chat Problem
slides.body:
At this age, social dynamics become more complex. Group chats can become weapons: being removed, being ignored, screenshots being shared. Signs your child is struggling:
• Obsessively checking their phone
• Mood crashes after screen time
• Refusing to go to school
• Saying ‘everyone hates me’

slides.heading: Scripts for Your Child
slides.body:
When they’re excluded from a party or gathering:
• ‘It’s okay to feel hurt — that IS hurtful’
• ‘Not being invited doesn’t mean not being valued’
• ‘What could you do this weekend that would make you feel good?’
• Help them plan something with a different friend

Don’t: call the other parents, post on social media, or badmouth the other kids.

slides.heading: The Quality vs Quantity Rule
slides.body:
Help your tween understand: you don’t need 15 friends. You need 2–3 people who genuinely care about you. Encourage them to invest in friendships where they feel:
• Safe being themselves
• Happy after spending time together (not drained)
• Supported, not judged
• Able to disagree without it being a disaster

activities.title: Tween Social Dynamics Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand what tweens are navigating socially.

cards.back: At 9–12, social dynamics move online. Group chats become weapons: being removed, ignored, or having screenshots shared. Watch for: obsessive phone checking, mood crashes after screen time, and withdrawal from family after being online.
Help your tween understand: you don't need 15 friends. You need 2–3 people who genuinely care about you — where you feel safe being yourself, happy after time together, supported rather than judged.

Puberty starts as early as 8. Bodies change at wildly different rates — being first or last creates intense self-consciousness. Focus on what bodies CAN DO, not how they look. Your own body comments are being carefully observed.

Watch for perfectionism: refusing to submit imperfect work, physical symptoms before tests, procrastination from fear of failure. Ask: 'Did you try your best?' not 'What did you get?' Celebrate effort and improvement, not grades.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of the tween years before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your knowledge of what 9–12 year olds are navigating and how to support them.

questions.question: What does the 'quality vs quantity' rule say about tween friendships?
options: More friendships mean more social resilience
Tweens need 2–3 genuine friendships more than a large social group
The number of friends matters as much as their quality
Tweens shouldn't have more than one close friend at a time
questions.explanation: Help tweens understand: they don't need 15 friends — they need 2–3 people who genuinely care about them. Chasing quantity (large social group) often means fitting in rather than genuine belonging.

questions.question: What is the most important thing NOT to say about a tween's appearance?
options: Commenting on their eye colour
Making comments about YOUR OWN body negatively
Telling them they look healthy and strong
Asking them what they'd like to wear
questions.explanation: Tweens absorb how their parents talk about their OWN bodies. Saying 'I'm so fat' or 'I look terrible' in front of a body-conscious 10-year-old teaches them exactly how to relate to their own body. Model body neutrality — your actions teach more than your words.

questions.question: What distinguishes healthy academic motivation from toxic pressure?
options: Healthy motivation involves getting top marks in all subjects
Healthy motivation is curiosity-driven; toxic pressure is fear-of-failure-driven
Healthy motivation requires parental monitoring of homework completion
Toxic pressure only comes from schools, not from parents
questions.explanation: Healthy motivation: 'I want to understand this.' Toxic pressure: 'I must be the best or I'm a failure.' The difference matters for long-term wellbeing — performance-orientation leads to burnout, mastery-orientation builds resilience.

questions.question: Why should you generally invite a concerning friend over rather than ban the friendship?
options: To monitor your child's behaviour around that friend
Banning usually makes the friend more appealing and pushes your child underground
To give the other child positive adult role modelling
Because banning is not legal for minor social relationships
questions.explanation: Banning friendships almost always backfires — it makes the forbidden friend more appealing and removes your visibility. Keeping them close gives you information and influence. Use curious questions to help your child evaluate the friendship themselves.

content.sentence: When your child is excluded from a party, say: 'It's okay to feel ___. Not being invited doesn't mean not being ___. What could you do this weekend that would make you feel ___?'

slides.heading: Why 9–12 Is Critical
slides.body: Puberty starts as early as 8 for some children. Bodies change at wildly different rates — being the first or last creates intense self-consciousness. At this age, children start comparing themselves to peers, celebrities, and social media images.

slides.heading: What NOT to Say
slides.body:
✘ ‘You look fine!’ (dismissive)
✘ ‘Don’t worry about your weight’ (introduces the concept)
✘ Comments about YOUR body (‘I’m so fat’ — they’re listening)
✘ ‘You’d be so pretty if you just...’
✘ Praising other kids’ appearances

✔ Instead: focus on what bodies CAN DO, not what they look like.

slides.heading: Build Body Respect
slides.body:
• Talk about bodies in terms of function: ‘Your legs are strong — they carried you up that hill!’
• Model body neutrality: eat without guilt, move for joy, dress for comfort
• Discuss how images are edited: ‘Let me show you what filters actually do’
• Celebrate diversity: different body types in media, sport, life
• If concerned about disordered eating, talk to your GP early

content.instruction: Match each body image scenario with the best response.
pairs: 'Am I fat?'
'Your body is strong and growing. What matters is how you feel, not how you look.'
You catch yourself saying 'I look terrible'
Reframe: 'I love what my body can do' — they're always listening
They compare themselves to an influencer
'Let me show you what filters actually do to photos'
They refuse to wear shorts in summer
Don't force it. 'You get to choose what you're comfortable in.'

slides.heading: Pressure vs Motivation
slides.body:
There’s a difference between healthy motivation (‘I want to do well’) and toxic pressure (‘I MUST be the best or I’m a failure’). Watch for:
• Perfectionism: refusing to submit work unless it’s flawless
• Procrastination: paralysed by fear of failure
• Physical symptoms: stomach aches before tests
• Cheating (to maintain impossible standards)

slides.heading: Homework Without Tears
slides.body:
• Create a consistent routine (same time, same place)
• Break work into chunks: ‘20 minutes on, 5 minutes off’
• Be nearby but don’t hover — available, not managing
• If they’re stuck: ‘What do you think the first step is?’ (don’t give answers)
• Let them experience natural consequences of forgotten homework occasionally — don’t rescue every time

slides.heading: Redefine Success
slides.body:
Ask: ‘Did you try your best?’ not ‘What did you get?’

Celebrate effort, improvement, curiosity — not grades.

‘I noticed you really pushed through that difficult chapter — that took real determination.’

Your child needs to know their worth isn’t attached to a number on a page.

content.question: Your 10-year-old is in tears because they got 78% on a test. They say ‘I’m so stupid.’ Best response?

options.label: ‘That’s a great mark! You should be proud!’
‘You’re clearly upset. What were you hoping for, and what felt hard about this test?’
‘Next time study harder and you’ll do better’

content.explanation: Validate the emotion and explore what’s behind it. Dismissing (‘great mark!’) ignores their feelings. ‘Study harder’ implies they didn’t try. ‘Marks don’t matter’ feels dishonest. Curiosity opens conversation.

lessons.title: When a Friend Is Being a Bad Influence

slides.heading: Don’t Ban the Friend
slides.body: Your first instinct may be to forbid the friendship. This almost always backfires — it makes the friend MORE appealing and pushes your child underground. Instead, keep the friend CLOSE: invite them over, get to know them, observe the dynamic.

slides.heading: Coach, Don’t Control
slides.body:
Ask curious questions:
• ‘What do you like about hanging out with Jake?’
• ‘How do you feel after spending time with him?’
• ‘Have you ever felt uncomfortable with something he’s suggested?’
• ‘What would you do if he wanted you to do something you weren’t sure about?’

Let THEM evaluate the friendship.

slides.heading: Red Line Conversations
slides.body:
There ARE situations where you step in:
• The friend introduces your child to substances
• There’s bullying or coercion happening
• Criminal activity is involved
• Your child’s personality is fundamentally changing

In these cases: ‘I’m not going to let you get hurt. This is a safety decision, not a punishment.’

content.scenario: Your 11-year-old has been spending time with a new friend who uses language you don't like and seems to encourage rule-breaking. Your child thinks this friend is 'cool.'

options.label: Ban the friendship: 'You're not allowed to see them anymore'
options.outcome: Banning almost always backfires — it makes the friend more appealing and pushes your child underground. You lose visibility into what's happening.

options.label: Invite the friend over, get to know them, observe the dynamic
options.outcome: Keeping them close gives you information and influence. You can coach your child with curious questions: 'How do you feel after hanging out with Jake?'

options.label: Ignore it and hope it passes
options.outcome: Some friendships do pass naturally. But if you're seeing behaviour changes, staying silent can feel like approval. Light-touch coaching is better than silence.

slides.heading: The Modern Talk
slides.body:
The ‘stranger danger’ talk now includes screens. At 9–12, children may be on gaming platforms, messaging apps, or social media where strangers can contact them. Be direct:
• ‘Some people online pretend to be kids but aren’t’
• ‘Never share personal info: school name, address, full name’
• ‘If anyone online makes you feel weird or asks for photos, tell me immediately — you won’t be in trouble’

slides.heading: Grooming Red Flags
slides.body:
Teach your child to recognise:
• Someone who gives them lots of compliments and attention
• Asks to keep their conversations secret
• Offers gifts, game credits, or money
• Asks them to move to a different platform
• Asks for photos or video
• Tries to isolate them from family/friends

Use real language: ‘Grooming is when an adult pretends to be your friend to get something from you.’

slides.heading: Create a No-Blame Policy
slides.body:
The single most important thing: your child must believe they can come to you WITHOUT getting in trouble. If they’ve broken a screen rule and encountered something scary, the LAST thing you want is for them to hide it because they’re afraid of your reaction.

‘If something makes you uncomfortable online, you tell me. I will NEVER be angry at you for telling me. I will always help you.’

content.statement: If your child encounters something scary online, the best approach is to take away their device as punishment.
content.explanation: If children fear punishment, they'll hide online problems instead of telling you. Create a no-blame policy: 'If something makes you uncomfortable online, tell me. I will NEVER be angry at you for telling me.'

slides.heading: Boredom Is Good For Them
slides.body: Research shows boredom drives creativity, self-direction, and resilience. Children who are constantly entertained never develop the ability to entertain themselves. When your child says ‘I’m bored,’ resist the urge to fix it.

slides.heading: What to Say
slides.body:
• ‘That’s great — your brain is about to come up with something interesting’
• ‘The boredom jar is on the shelf’ (jar of activity ideas they’ve written)
• ‘You have 15 minutes. If you’re still bored after that, I’ve got some chores’
• Don’t: hand them a screen, plan an activity, feel guilty

slides.heading: Build Independent Play
slides.body:
Set up conditions for self-directed time:
• Art supplies accessible (not hidden)
• Building materials (cardboard, tape, sticks)
• Books everywhere
• A ‘quiet time’ routine: 30–60 minutes daily of no screens, no parental entertainment
• Get comfortable with them being uncomfortable — this is where growth happens

content.question: Your 10-year-old says 'I'm SO BORED' for the fifth time today. Best response?

options.label: Hand them a tablet to keep them quiet
'That's great — your brain is about to come up with something interesting'
Plan an activity for them immediately
'You have a room full of toys — how can you be bored?!'

content.explanation: Research shows boredom drives creativity and self-direction. Resist the urge to fix it. Children who learn to manage boredom develop stronger internal resources.

lessons.title: Peer Pressure to Try Drugs or Alcohol

activities.title: Teen Safety Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore high-stakes teenage situations, take a moment to check in.

content.question: How prepared do you feel for the difficult conversations you might need to have with your teenager?

slides.heading: Have the Talk EARLY
slides.body:
Don’t wait until they’re offered something. Start at 11–12 with age-appropriate facts:
• Alcohol affects the developing brain differently than adult brains
• Cannabis is NOT harmless for teenagers — it affects memory, motivation, and developing neural pathways
• Vaping is not ‘just water vapour’

Be factual, not dramatic. Scare tactics don’t work — they just stop telling you things.

slides.heading: Exit Scripts
slides.body:
Role-play BEFORE it happens. Give them scripts:
• ‘Nah, I’m good’ (casual, no explanation needed)
• ‘I’ve got training tomorrow’ (blame sport/activity)
• ‘My parents drug test me’ (use you as the excuse — give permission for this)
• ‘I’m on medication that doesn’t mix with it’
• Hold a drink/cup to avoid being offered one

The code word system: text PIZZA and you come get them, no questions asked.

slides.heading: If They’ve Already Tried Something
slides.body:
If they tell you (or you find out):
• First: breathe. Your reaction determines whether they’ll tell you next time.
• ‘Thank you for telling me. That took courage.’
• ‘Help me understand — what was the situation?’
• Focus on safety, not punishment: ‘If you’re ever in a situation where you’ve had something and you need a ride, call me. No questions in the car.’
• THEN have the boundaries conversation.

activities.title: Teen Safety Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the core principles for keeping teenagers safe.

cards.back: Have substance conversations at 11–12, before they're offered anything. Be factual, not dramatic. Scare tactics don't work — they just make teens stop telling you things. Give real, age-appropriate information about how substances affect the developing brain.

Role-play refusal scripts before they're needed: 'Nah, I'm good.' 'My parents drug test me.' 'I've got training tomorrow.' Give them permission to use you as the excuse. Scripts rehearsed at home are available under social pressure.

The most protective thing you can offer: 'If you're ever in a situation where you've had something and need a ride, call me. No questions in the car.' Your first reaction determines whether they'll call you next time they need help.

A pre-agreed code word or text = pick me up immediately, no questions asked tonight. Works for parties, unsafe cars, uncomfortable situations. Honour the deal every time — even at 2am. Debrief the next day, calmly.

content.statement: The most effective approach to preventing teenage substance use is showing them graphic images of drug damage.
content.explanation: Research consistently shows scare tactics are ineffective and can actually increase curiosity. Open, honest conversations about real risks, combined with strong family connection and rehearsed exit strategies, are far more effective.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test your understanding of navigating high-stakes teen situations.

content.intro: Let's check your knowledge of keeping teenagers safe while maintaining connection.

questions.question: Why do scare tactics about substance use generally NOT work with teenagers?
options: Because teenagers don't understand the health consequences
Because teenagers are attracted to danger and scare tactics make substances seem more appealing
Because research shows scare tactics are ineffective and make teens less likely to talk to you
Because the images used in scare campaigns are not graphic enough
questions.explanation: Research consistently shows scare tactics (graphic images, exaggerated consequences) are ineffective and can increase curiosity. They also damage trust, making teens less likely to come to you if they encounter problems. Honest, accurate conversations work better.

questions.question: What age should substance conversations ideally begin?
options: Only when they ask about it
At age 15–16 when peer pressure peaks
At age 11–12, before they're likely to be offered anything
At age 18 when they are legally an adult
questions.explanation: Conversations should begin at 11–12 — before the high-risk peer pressure period. Starting early with age-appropriate facts means your child already has accurate information and open communication with you before they need it.

questions.question: If your teenager calls to tell you they've tried something at a party, what is the most important first response?
options: Express that you're very disappointed
Ask them to stay where they are while you call other parents
Stay calm and say 'Thank you for telling me. That took courage.'
Ask them exactly what they took and how much
questions.explanation: Your first reaction determines whether they'll call you next time. Expressing disappointment immediately teaches them NOT to tell you in future situations. Gratitude for honesty, combined with genuine care for their safety, keeps communication open.

questions.question: What should happen when your teen uses the code word?
options: You call them to get details before going to pick them up
You go immediately, stay calm in the car, save all conversation for the next day
You text back asking if they are in trouble first
You send another trusted adult so you can both debrief in the car
questions.explanation: When the code word is used: go immediately, say nothing significant in the car except 'I'm glad you called me,' and debrief calmly the next day. Any violation of the 'no questions tonight' agreement may prevent them using the code word next time.

lessons.title: A Friend Pressures Them to Drive Drunk (or Get in a Car)

slides.heading: The Non-Negotiable Rule
slides.body:
This is one of the few parenting hills to die on. Make it crystal clear:
• ‘You NEVER get in a car with someone who has been drinking. Ever.’
• ‘You NEVER drive after drinking. Ever.’
• ‘I will come get you from ANYWHERE at ANY time with NO punishment for calling me.’

Say this repeatedly. Make it a family mantra.

slides.heading: How to Get Out
slides.body:
Practical exit strategies:
• Code word text to parent = immediate pick-up
• Pre-download a ride-share app with your payment card
• ‘My mum tracks my location — she’ll know if I’m in a car’
• Call ANY family member or trusted adult
• Walk if it’s safe, or go to the nearest open business

Practice saying: ‘I’m going to find another way home.’

slides.heading: After the Situation
slides.body:
If they call you at 2am from a party:
• Go get them. Say NOTHING in the car (except ‘I’m glad you called me’).
• Talk the next day when everyone is calm.
• ‘I’m proud of you for making the safe choice. That was hard.’
• THEN discuss any other issues (were they drinking? were they somewhere they shouldn’t have been?)

The message: safety first, consequences second.

content.sentence: When your teen wants to go to a party, respond with: 'I want to say ___ but I need to know: who's ___, where is it, what time will you be ___, and how are you getting ___?'

slides.heading: The Facts
slides.body: By age 17, approximately 1 in 4 teenagers has sent or received a sexually explicit image. This is a reality parents MUST address. In most countries, sharing intimate images of minors is a criminal offence — even if the person in the photo sent it themselves.

slides.heading: Prevention Scripts
slides.body:
Have this conversation directly:
• ‘If someone asks for a nude photo, the answer is always no — no matter how much you trust them’
• ‘Screenshots exist. Images can be shared in seconds.’
• ‘If someone sends you an image, don’t forward it. That’s potentially a crime.’
• ‘If someone pressures you, that’s a red flag about THEM, not about you.’

Exit line: ‘Sorry, that’s not my thing’ or simply ‘No.’

slides.heading: If It’s Already Happened
slides.body:
If your teen’s image has been shared:
• Stay calm (they’re already terrified)
• ‘This is not your fault. The person who shared it is responsible.’
• Screenshot evidence before anything is deleted
• Report to the platform
• Contact the school if classmates are involved
• Consider contacting police (non-emergency) for advice
• Seek support: this can cause significant emotional distress

content.title: When They Break a Rule

columnB.label: Responsive (Effective)
items: 'You made a bad choice. You're not a bad person.'

content.reflection: Think of the last time your teen broke a rule. Which column did your response fall into?

slides.heading: Warning Signs
slides.body:
Take these seriously — even if they seem ‘attention-seeking’ (attention-seeking IS a call for help):
• Withdrawal from friends, family, activities
• Changes in sleep, appetite, energy
• Giving away possessions
• Talking about being a burden
• Unexplained marks or long sleeves in summer
• Saying ‘What’s the point?’ or ‘I wish I wasn’t here’
• Sudden calmness after a period of depression (can indicate a decision has been made)

slides.heading: How to Ask the Hard Question
slides.body:
Asking about suicide does NOT plant the idea. Research is clear on this.

Say directly: ‘Are you thinking about hurting yourself?’ or ‘Are you having thoughts about not wanting to be alive?’

If yes:
• Stay calm
• ‘I’m really glad you told me. You’re not alone.’
• Remove access to means (medications, sharp objects)
• Don’t leave them alone
• Call your local crisis line or take them to the emergency department

slides.heading: Self-Harm Is Communication
slides.body:
Self-harm (cutting, burning, hitting themselves) is usually NOT a suicide attempt — it’s a coping mechanism for overwhelming emotions. Do not react with horror or anger.

• ‘I can see you’re in a lot of pain. I want to help.’
• Don’t demand they stop immediately (they need alternative coping strategies first)
• Seek professional support (GP referral to a psychologist or counsellor)
• NZ Crisis: Need to Talk? Free call or text 1737

content.prompt: Do you know your local crisis numbers? Does your teen know they can talk to you about dark thoughts without being judged? Write down your family’s mental health safety plan.

slides.heading: Take It Seriously
slides.body:
A 14-year-old’s heartbreak is as real as an adult’s. Their brain processes it with the same intensity. Never say:
✘ ‘You’ll get over it’
✘ ‘You’re too young for a relationship’
✘ ‘There are plenty more fish’

✔ ‘This really hurts, doesn’t it? I’m here.’
✔ ‘Tell me about what you liked about this person.’
✔ ‘Heartbreak is one of the hardest things. It won’t always feel this intense.’

slides.heading: Teaching Healthy Relationship Signs
slides.body:
Teach these BEFORE they start dating:

✔ Healthy: respects your boundaries, supports your friendships, communicates openly, makes you feel good about yourself

✘ Unhealthy: jealous, controlling, isolating you from friends/family, monitoring your phone, making you feel like you’re never good enough, guilt-tripping

‘A person who loves you will never make you feel afraid.’

slides.heading: The Consent Conversation
slides.body:
Be direct and ongoing:
• ‘You have the right to say no at ANY point — even if you said yes before’
• ‘If someone is too drunk/high to clearly say yes, that’s a no’
• ‘A real partner respects boundaries without sulking’
• ‘Pressure is not love’

This conversation isn’t one-off. It’s ongoing, casual, and normalised.

content.scenario: It's 11pm on a Saturday. Your 15-year-old texts the code word 'PIZZA' — your agreed signal that they need picking up, no questions asked.

options.label: Go immediately, stay calm, save the conversation for tomorrow
options.outcome: This is exactly how the system should work. They used the code word, which means they trusted you. Interrogating them in the car breaks that trust. Tomorrow, gently: 'I'm glad you texted. Want to talk about it?'

options.label: Call them and demand to know what happened before you drive
options.outcome: This defeats the purpose of a no-questions code word. Next time they'll think twice about using it — and might stay in an unsafe situation instead.

options.label: Text back 'What happened? Are you in trouble?'
options.outcome: Even texting questions can feel like pressure. The deal was: text PIZZA, get picked up, no questions tonight. Honour the deal.

slides.heading: It’s Usually Not Laziness
slides.body:
A teenager refusing school is almost always communicating something deeper:
• Anxiety (social or academic)
• Bullying they haven’t disclosed
• Learning difficulties (they’d rather look ‘bad’ than ‘dumb’)
• Depression
• Not fitting in
• Conflict with a teacher

Don’t start with ‘you HAVE to go.’ Start with: ‘Help me understand what’s making school so hard right now.’

slides.heading: The Re-Engagement Plan
slides.body:
If they’ve been away:
1. Meet with the school (pastoral care, dean, counsellor)
2. Start with partial attendance (just mornings, just favourite subjects)
3. Identify one adult at school they trust
4. Address the underlying issue (therapy if needed)
5. Small wins: ‘You went for two hours today. That took real courage.’

Don’t: threaten, bribe, or make them feel worse for struggling.

slides.heading: When They Just Don’t Care
slides.body:
Some teens lose motivation without anxiety — they’re just... disconnected. This often signals:
• They don’t see the relevance
• They’re overwhelmed and have shut down
• Depression
• They need autonomy (being controlled = checking out)

Try: ‘What DO you care about? Let’s figure out how to connect that to your future.’

content.statement: Giving your teenager privacy means you should never check their phone or social media.
content.explanation: Privacy is earned and age-appropriate. Younger teens need more oversight, gradually reducing as they prove trustworthy. The key: be transparent about it. 'I respect your privacy AND I have a responsibility to keep you safe. Here's how we'll balance that.'

slides.heading: This Is Normal Development
slides.body: Adolescence is THE time for identity exploration — this includes gender, sexuality, beliefs, values, style, and life direction. Your teen trying on different identities isn’t a phase to be corrected — it’s the developmental task of adolescence.

slides.heading: If Your Child Comes Out
slides.body:
What they need to hear:
• ‘Thank you for trusting me with this.’
• ‘I love you. Nothing changes that.’
• ‘What do you need from me?’

What NOT to do:
• Don’t say ‘Are you sure?’ or ‘It’s just a phase’
• Don’t out them to other family members without permission
• Don’t make it about your feelings (process YOUR emotions separately)
• Don’t try to change them

slides.heading: If You’re Struggling
slides.body:
It’s okay if this wasn’t what you expected. It’s okay to need time to adjust. What matters is:
• Your child’s safety and mental health
• Research shows family acceptance is THE strongest protective factor against depression and suicide in LGBTQ+ youth
• Get support for yourself (parent groups, counselling) so you can show up for your child
• Their identity is not a reflection of your parenting

content.instruction: When your teen is struggling emotionally, put these responses in the right order:
items: Ask what they need from you
Offer perspective or advice (only if asked)
Follow up later to check in
correctOrder: Listen without trying to fix
Validate their feelings
Ask what they need from you
Offer perspective or advice (only if asked)
Follow up later to check in

slides.heading: Before the Party
slides.body:
Every time your teen goes to a party, ask:
• Where is it?
• Whose house? (contact the parents)
• Who else is going?
• Will there be alcohol?
• How will you get home?
• What time will you be back?

Yes, they’ll roll their eyes. Do it anyway. Frame it as: ‘This is what caring looks like.’

slides.heading: The Safety Toolkit
slides.body:
Give them practical tools:
• Phone charged, location sharing on
• Cash for emergencies
• Code word = pick me up immediately
• Never leave your drink unattended
• Stick with friends, leave with friends
• If something feels wrong, LEAVE
• ‘You can always use me as an excuse: Mum said I have to be home by 11’

slides.heading: If You’re Hosting
slides.body:
If the party is at YOUR house:
• Be visible but not hovering
• No alcohol for under-18s (you’re legally liable)
• Lock away your own alcohol and medications
• Have food and non-alcoholic drinks available
• Know who’s there and how they’re getting home
• Have a clear end time
• Check the garden/bedrooms periodically

content.sentence: When your teen says 'You don't understand!', try: 'You're right — I might not fully ___. Help me ___. I'm not here to ___ you, I'm here to ___ you.'

activities.title: Difficult Situations Check-In
activities.instruction: Before we explore difficult family situations, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How confident do you feel supporting your child through major life changes or family upheaval?

slides.heading: What Children Need to Hear
slides.body:
• ‘This is NOT your fault. You didn’t cause this.’
• ‘Both of us love you just as much as always.’
• ‘You don’t have to choose sides.’
• ‘It’s okay to feel sad, angry, confused — all of those feelings are valid.’
• ‘We’ll figure this out together, and here’s what’s staying the same: [school, friends, sports, bedtime routine].’

slides.heading: The Golden Rules
slides.body:
• NEVER badmouth the other parent in front of your child
• Don’t use your child as a messenger
• Don’t pump them for information about the other parent
• Don’t compete for their love with gifts or leniency
• Keep routines as consistent as possible between houses
• Let them love both parents freely

Your child is not your therapist. Get adult support for your own pain.

slides.heading: Age-Specific Reactions
slides.body:
5–8: May blame themselves, regress (bedwetting, clinginess), act out
9–12: May take sides, feel responsible for fixing it, anger at both parents
13–17: May withdraw, act out, rush into relationships of their own

All of these are NORMAL grief responses. Patience, consistency, and professional support if needed.

Child is anxious without their device
Gradual exposure — start with 30 min phone-free
They're watching inappropriate content
Open conversation, not punishment — 'Tell me what you saw'
