activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect on your own experience.

content.question: How comfortable do you feel talking to your child about death or significant loss?

slides.heading: Children Grieve Differently
slides.body: Children don’t grieve in a straight line. They may seem fine one moment and devastated the next. They may grieve in ‘puddles’ — short, intense bursts followed by playing and seeming normal. This doesn’t mean they don’t care. It means their developing brain processes grief in doses.

slides.heading: What to Say (And Not Say)
slides.body:
✔ ‘Grandpa died. His body stopped working.’ (clear, honest)
✔ ‘It’s okay to cry. It’s okay to not cry too.’
✔ ‘I feel sad too. We can be sad together.’

✘ ‘They’re in a better place’ (why would a better place be away from me?)
✘ ‘Be strong’ (teaches them to suppress grief)
✘ ‘They went to sleep’ (creates fear of bedtime)

slides.heading: Use Metaphor-Based Stories
slides.body:
Sometimes the right words are hard to find, especially when you’re grieving too. The Little Minds Big Questions tool creates gentle, age-appropriate metaphor stories about death, loss, and difficult topics.

Ask a question like: ‘Why did grandma have to die?’ and receive a warm, child-friendly story that helps them process.

Visit: littleminds.mindcast.co.nz

activities.title: Children & Grief: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to explore how children experience and process loss differently from adults.

cards.back: Children grieve in 'puddles' — short, intense bursts of emotion followed by playing and seeming totally fine. This is healthy and normal. It doesn't mean they don't care; it means their developing brain processes grief in manageable doses.

Use clear, honest words: 'Grandpa died. His body stopped working.' Avoid: 'went to sleep' (causes bedtime fear), 'passed away' (abstract), 'in a better place' (confusing — why would a better place be away from me?). Honesty builds trust during hard times.
Young children may believe their thoughts or actions caused the death. 'Did grandma die because I was naughty?' is a real fear. Always reassure: 'Nothing you did caused this. It is not your fault.'

Grief resurfaces at developmental milestones — birthdays, graduations, sports days. Children may re-grieve as they mature and can understand more. A child who seemed 'over it' at 6 may be deeply sad about the same loss at 12.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of supporting children through grief and loss.

questions.question: What does 'puddle grief' mean in children?
options: They cry in the bath
Short bursts of grief followed by normal play — a healthy processing pattern
They only grieve if they see water
They suppress all emotions
questions.explanation: Children grieve in 'puddles' — intense moments of emotion followed by play. This is developmentally appropriate and doesn't mean they aren't affected.

questions.question: Which phrase should be AVOIDED when telling a child about death?
options: 'Grandpa died — his body stopped working.'
'It's okay to cry and it's okay not to cry.'
'They went to sleep and won't wake up.'
'I feel sad too — we can be sad together.'
questions.explanation: 'They went to sleep' links death to sleep and can create intense bedtime fear. Use clear, honest language like 'died' and 'his body stopped working.'

questions.question: Why might a child feel they caused a death?
options: Children are naturally selfish
Magical thinking — young children believe their thoughts or actions can cause events
They watch too much TV
They don't understand death at all
questions.explanation: Young children engage in magical thinking and may genuinely believe bad thoughts or behaviour caused the loss. Always reassure them directly: 'Nothing you did caused this.'

questions.question: When might grief resurface for a child who seemed 'over it'?
options: Never — once resolved, grief is done
Only if they see a photo of the person who died
At developmental milestones as they gain new understanding
Only in teenagers
questions.explanation: Grief resurfaces at milestones like birthdays, graduations, or major life events. Children re-grieve with new depth as they mature and develop greater understanding.

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?

content.question: How confident are you in encouraging your daughter's self-worth without focusing on her appearance?

slides.heading: Stop Praising Pretty
slides.body:
The first thing most adults say to a girl: ‘You’re so pretty/cute!’ The message: your appearance is your most notable quality.

Instead: ‘What are you reading?’ ‘Tell me about your project’ ‘You seem like you’ve been thinking hard about something.’

Praise effort, curiosity, kindness, courage — not appearance.

slides.heading: Model Imperfection
slides.body:
Your daughter is watching how YOU handle:
• Making mistakes (‘I messed up. Here’s what I learned.’)
• Your body (‘I love what my body can do’ — not ‘I look fat’)
• Conflict (‘I disagreed and stood my ground’)
• Saying no (‘I can’t do that this week’ — without guilt)
• Taking up space (‘I have something to say’)

She will do what you DO, not what you SAY.

slides.heading: Encourage Risk-Taking
slides.body:
Girls are socialised to be careful. Boys are told ‘you’ll be fine.’ Consciously:
• Let her climb higher
• Let her speak up in class (practise at dinner table first)
• Let her fail — and recover
• Encourage her to negotiate (pocket money, bedtime)
• Don’t rescue her from discomfort
• ‘That was brave’ > ‘Be careful’

activities.title: Building Girl Confidence: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to discover what the research says about raising confident girls.

cards.back: Complimenting girls primarily on looks teaches them their most notable quality is how they look. Instead, praise effort, curiosity, courage, and kindness. Ask: 'What are you working on?' and 'What did you learn?'

Girls are socialised to be careful while boys are told 'you'll be fine.' Consciously encourage your daughter to climb higher, speak up in class, fail, and recover. 'That was brave' is more powerful than 'Be careful.'

Your daughter is watching how YOU handle mistakes, your body, conflict, and saying no. She will do what you DO, not what you SAY. Every time you model imperfection without shame, you give her permission to do the same.

Perfectionism is often 'anxiety wearing an achievement costume.' Girls who won't try unless they're certain to succeed, erase homework repeatedly, or catastrophise small mistakes may be struggling with anxiety — not just high standards.

content.title: Praising Girls: Old Way vs New Way
content.reflection: Notice which phrases you default to this week.

activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of raising confident girls.

questions.question: What does research show is the impact of primarily complimenting girls on their appearance?
options: It builds their confidence and self-worth
It teaches them that appearance is their most notable quality
It has no measurable effect
It only affects girls under age 5
questions.explanation: When the first thing adults say to girls is about how they look, the message is that appearance is their most important quality. Instead, praise effort, curiosity, courage, and kindness.

questions.question: What is 'perfectionism' often described as in girls?
options: A healthy drive for excellence
Anxiety wearing an achievement costume
A sign of high intelligence
A sign of laziness
questions.explanation: Perfectionism is frequently 'anxiety wearing an achievement costume.' Girls who won't try new things, erase work repeatedly, or catastrophise small mistakes are often managing underlying anxiety, not just high standards.

questions.question: How can parents best encourage risk-taking in daughters?
options: Protect them from failure at all costs
Model your own risk-taking and allow them to fail and recover
Tell them stories about other girls who succeeded
Reduce expectations so they're less afraid
questions.explanation: Girls are socialised to be careful. Parents can counteract this by modelling risk-taking themselves, allowing daughters to fail and recover, and praising courage over caution.

questions.question: What matters MORE than what you SAY to your daughter about self-worth?
options: How often you say it
What you DO — how you model handling mistakes, your body, and conflict
Which books you read to her
How her teachers respond to her
questions.explanation: Children watch what their parents DO under pressure. If you handle your own mistakes with shame or talk negatively about your body, she absorbs that — regardless of what you tell her to believe.

content.question: How prepared do you feel to support your daughter through complex girl friendship dynamics?

slides.heading: Relational Aggression
slides.body: Girls are more likely to bully through relationships: exclusion, gossip, silent treatment, social media manipulation. This is often invisible to adults but devastating to the target. Don’t dismiss it as ‘girls being girls.’

slides.heading: Help Her Recognise Toxic Friendships
slides.body:
Teach her the friendship audit:
• ‘Do you feel better or worse after spending time with this person?’
• ‘Can you be yourself around them?’
• ‘Do they support your other friendships or try to control them?’
• ‘Do they keep your secrets safe?’
• ‘Would you treat someone the way they treat you?’

slides.heading: When She IS the Mean Girl
slides.body:
This is harder to hear, but sometimes your daughter is the one causing harm. If this happens:
• Don’t defend or deny (‘My child would never...’)
• ‘Help me understand what’s going on for you that you’re acting this way’
• Address the root: insecurity, home stress, social pressure
• Require repair: genuine apology, changed behaviour
• Monitor without hovering

activities.title: Girl Friendship Dynamics: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand how to support your daughter through girl friendship challenges.

cards.back: Girls are more likely to bully through relationships: exclusion, gossip, silent treatment, and social media manipulation. This is often invisible to adults but devastating to the target. Don't dismiss it as 'girls being girls' — it causes real harm.

Teach your daughter to ask: 'Do I feel better or worse after spending time with this person?' 'Can I be myself around them?' 'Do they support my other friendships or try to control them?' 'Would I treat someone the way they treat me?'

cards.front: When She IS the Mean Girl
cards.back: If your daughter is causing harm, don't defend or deny. Ask: 'Help me understand what's going on for you that you're acting this way.' Address the root — insecurity, home stress, social pressure. Require genuine apology and changed behaviour.

cards.front: Parent Involvement: When to Step In
cards.back: For most friendship dramas, coach your daughter to handle it herself. Parent intervention should be a last resort. Step in when: there's persistent bullying, safety concerns, or when the school needs to be involved.

content.scenario: Your 12-year-old daughter comes home in tears. Her best friend has been spreading rumours about her and turned the group against her.

options.label: 'That's awful. Tell me everything. Let's figure out what YOU want to do.'
options.outcome: Empowering her to choose her response builds agency. She might want to confront the friend, distance herself, or talk to a teacher. Support her choice while coaching through the options.

options.label: 'I'm calling her mother right now!'
options.outcome: This removes your daughter's agency and may escalate the situation. Parent intervention should be a last resort for social conflicts at this age.

options.label: 'Girls are just like that — it'll blow over'
options.outcome: Dismissing relational aggression as normal minimises her pain. It IS normal developmentally but it's still harmful and deserves your attention.

questions.question: What is 'relational aggression'?
options: Physical fighting between girls
Bullying through relationships — exclusion, gossip, silent treatment, and social manipulation
Girls who are overly competitive in sports
A healthy form of peer competition
questions.explanation: Relational aggression is when girls use relationships as weapons: excluding, spreading rumours, silent treatment, or social media manipulation. It's often invisible to adults but causes serious harm.

questions.question: When your daughter experiences friendship betrayal, your FIRST response should be:
options: Call the other parent immediately
Tell her it's normal and will blow over
Validate her feelings and ask what SHE wants to do
Contact the school
questions.explanation: Empowering your daughter to choose her own response builds agency and problem-solving skills. Validate her feelings first, then explore options together — she may want to confront, distance, or forgive.

questions.question: If you discover your daughter is being the 'mean girl,' the best first step is:
options: Dismiss the claim — 'My child would never do that'
Punish her immediately
Be curious: 'Help me understand what's going on for you that you're acting this way'
Change her school
questions.explanation: Curiosity before judgment helps you address the root cause — often insecurity, stress, or social pressure. Then require genuine apology and behavioural change.

questions.question: The friendship audit question 'Do I feel better or worse after spending time with this person?' helps girls:
options: Pick the most popular friends
Identify whether a friendship is healthy or draining
Avoid conflict at all costs
Find friends who always agree with them
questions.explanation: Teaching girls to check in with how friendships feel — energising or draining, safe or anxious — helps them make better long-term friendship choices based on wellbeing rather than status.

content.question: How comfortable are you talking about emotions openly with your son?

slides.heading: The Shutdown Starts Early
slides.body:
By age 5, boys have already learned to suppress emotions. Research shows:
• Boys are told ‘don’t cry’ or ‘toughen up’ far more than girls
• Parents use fewer emotional words with sons
• Boys’ pain is taken less seriously
• By adolescence, many boys can only express one emotion: anger (because it’s the only one that feels ‘acceptable’)

slides.heading: What to Do Instead
slides.body:
• Name emotions: ‘It looks like you’re feeling frustrated’
• Normalise crying: ‘Crying is your body’s way of releasing big feelings. That’s healthy.’
• Model vulnerability: ‘I felt really sad today when...’
• Don’t use gendered emotion language: ‘Boys don’t cry’ / ‘Man up’
• Create safe spaces: car rides, bedtime, one-on-one walks
• Ask open questions: ‘What was the best/hardest part of your day?’

slides.heading: Communication With Teenage Boys
slides.body:
Teenage boys communicate differently:
• They talk while DOING something (not face-to-face)
• They speak in short bursts (don’t push for more)
• They process internally first (give them time)
• They respond to genuine interest, not interrogation

Best conversation triggers: cooking, driving, gaming together, physical activity side by side.

‘Grunt’ is a language. Learn it. The connection is still there.

activities.title: Boys & Emotions: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand how emotional conditioning affects boys and what to do instead.

cards.back: By age 5, boys have already learned to suppress emotions. Parents use fewer emotional words with sons, boys' pain is taken less seriously, and by adolescence many boys can only safely express one emotion: anger — because it's the only one that feels acceptable.

Naming emotions reduces their intensity. Try: 'It looks like you're feeling frustrated' or 'That sounds really disappointing.' Boys who develop an emotional vocabulary are more resilient and have better relationships throughout life.

Teen boys communicate best while DOING something — not face-to-face. Car rides, cooking, gaming together, physical activity side by side. They talk in short bursts, process internally first, and respond to genuine interest rather than interrogation.

If you never cry, never express sadness, never say 'I'm struggling' — your son learns that emotional suppression is what men do. Sharing age-appropriate emotions ('I felt really sad today when...') is more powerful than any lecture on feelings.

content.sentence: Instead of saying 'Man up' or 'Boys don't ___', try: 'It looks like you're feeling ___. Crying is your body's way of releasing big ___. That's ___.'

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of raising emotionally intelligent boys.

questions.question: By what age have most boys already learned to suppress emotions?
options: Age 2
Age 5

questions.explanation: Research shows boys have already learned to suppress emotions by age 5. They are told 'don't cry' more often than girls, their pain is taken less seriously, and emotional language is used less around them from early on.

questions.question: By adolescence, what is often the ONLY emotion boys feel safe expressing?
options: Sadness
Fear
Anger
Joy
questions.explanation: Many adolescent boys can only safely express anger because it's the only 'acceptable' emotion under masculine conditioning. Sadness, fear, and vulnerability are suppressed — often leading to explosiveness under pressure.

questions.question: When do teenage boys communicate best?
options: In formal sit-down conversations
When doing something side-by-side, not face-to-face
When asked direct questions
During family meetings
questions.explanation: Teen boys communicate best while doing something — car rides, cooking, gaming, physical activity. Face-to-face conversations feel like interrogation. Side-by-side activity reduces pressure and opens up genuine conversation.

questions.question: What is the most powerful thing a parent can do to teach emotional expression to their son?
options: Buy him books about emotions
Put him in therapy
Model emotional expression themselves
Create a feeling chart on the fridge
questions.explanation: Children do what we do, not what we say. If you share your own emotions, cry, and say 'I'm struggling today,' your son learns that emotional expression is healthy and safe for men. This is more powerful than any conversation about feelings.

content.question: How confident do you feel answering the 'hard questions' your child asks about death, sex, money, or difficult life topics?

slides.heading: Why Metaphors Work
slides.body:
Children’s brains are wired for stories, not lectures. When you explain death as ‘the body stopped working,’ they understand intellectually. But when you tell them ‘it’s like a leaf that falls from a tree in autumn — the tree remembers every leaf,’ they understand EMOTIONALLY.

Metaphors bypass resistance and create understanding at a deeper level.

slides.heading: Common Hard Questions
slides.body:
Questions that catch parents off guard:
• ‘Why did Grandpa die?’
• ‘What happens when you die?’
• ‘Why are you and Daddy fighting?’
• ‘Why is that person homeless?’
• ‘Am I fat?’
• ‘Why do people have different skin colours?’
• ‘Where do babies come from?’
• ‘Why can’t we afford that?’

You don’t need perfect answers. You need honest, gentle, age-appropriate ones.

slides.heading: Little Minds Big Questions
slides.body:
When you’re stuck for words, use the Little Minds tool. It creates warm, age-appropriate metaphor-based stories to help your child understand:

• Death & grief
• Feelings & emotions
• Family changes
• Fairness & justice
• The body
• Friendships

Just type your child’s question and get a gentle story you can share together.

Visit: littleminds.mindcast.co.nz

content.question: How would you rate your child's motivation and engagement with their own education right now?

slides.heading: The Ownership Shift
slides.body: Children who see education as THEIR project (not yours) are more motivated. Stop asking 'Did you do your homework?' and start asking 'What's your plan for tonight?' The shift from monitoring to coaching changes everything.

slides.heading: The Switch Point Metaphor
slides.body: Every small decision is like a railway switch — just three inches of steel that sends you hundreds of miles in one direction or another. Help your teen see that daily choices about study, effort, and showing up are switch points for their future. Not dramatic — just true.

slides.heading: When They're Failing
slides.body:
Before you panic:
• Ask: 'What's going on?' (not 'Why are you failing?')
• Investigate: learning difficulty? social issue? depression? wrong subject?
• Separate the person from the grade: 'You are not your marks'
• Problem-solve together: 'What would help? A tutor? A study group? A different approach?'
• Let natural consequences teach when appropriate

activities.title: School Motivation: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to discover what drives genuine academic engagement.

cards.back: Children who see education as THEIR project are more motivated than those whose parents monitor and push. Shift from 'Did you do your homework?' to 'What's your plan for tonight?' This moves from monitoring to coaching — and changes everything.

Every small daily decision is like a railway switch — just three inches of steel that sends you hundreds of miles in a different direction. Help your teen see that daily choices about effort and showing up are switch points for their future.

Performance-oriented students ('I need an A') burn out faster — every test becomes a judgment of worth. Mastery-oriented students ('I want to understand this') are more resilient because they're driven by curiosity, not fear. Shift 'What did you get?' to 'What did you learn?'

Before panicking about poor grades: Ask 'What's going on?' (not 'Why are failing?'). Investigate whether there's a learning difficulty, social issue, mental health concern, or wrong subject. Separate the person from the grade: 'You are not your marks.'

'Fine, but you still need to pass.'

content.explanation: Curiosity opens dialogue. When you explore their interest, you can naturally connect it to real skills (editing, marketing, communication, business) that school CAN support. Dismissing dreams closes the conversation entirely.

content.question: How well do you know what truly lights your child up — beyond grades and performance?

slides.heading: Beyond Academics
slides.body:
Not every child thrives in traditional schooling. Help them find their 'thing':
• What do they lose track of time doing?
• What topics do they choose to read/watch about?
• What would they do if no one was watching or judging?
• What problem in the world bothers them most?

Their 'thing' might be music, coding, cooking, sport, art, activism — it doesn't have to look like a traditional career path.

slides.heading: The 10-Year Vision
slides.body:
Try this exercise with your teen: 'Introduce yourself as you'd like to be 10 years from now. Where do you live? What do you do? What matters to you?'

This isn't about pressure — it's about possibility. When they can see a future worth working toward, daily motivation follows naturally.

Whatever your teen is passionate about connects to real, marketable skills. Gaming: strategy, teamwork, coding. YouTube: communication, editing, marketing. Cooking: creativity, business, nutrition. Help them see the path from passion to competence.

Purpose doesn't have to be grand. A teenager who volunteers at a dog shelter, builds a community garden, or tutors younger students finds meaning — and motivation follows meaning. Help them connect to something bigger than grades.

content.question: How confident are you in helping your child choose friends who are a positive influence?

slides.heading: Steady vs Fickle Friends
slides.body:
Teach your child the difference:

Steady friends: like you for who you are, stick around when things are hard, keep your secrets, celebrate your wins without jealousy.

Fickle friends: like you for what you have or who you know, drop you when someone 'better' comes along, use your secrets as weapons.

Ask: 'Would this person still be your friend if you lost everything popular about you?'

slides.heading: The Popularity Trap
slides.body:
Popularity isn't good or bad — it depends on WHY someone is popular. Some people are well-liked because they're genuinely kind and capable. Others are 'popular' because people are afraid of them.

Help your teen see: real influence comes from character, not status. The kids who are comfortable being themselves — not trying to climb the social ladder — often end up happiest.

slides.heading: Don't Centre Your Life on Friends
slides.body:
Friends make a terrible 'centre of gravity' for your life — they're imperfect, changeable, and human. If your self-worth depends on your friend count or how they treat you today, you'll be an emotional rollercoaster.

Better centre: your own values. When you know what you stand for, friendships become something you enjoy — not something you desperately need.

content.question: How comfortable are you coaching your child through serious friendship conflicts like betrayal or gossip?

slides.heading: When a Friend Betrays You
slides.body:
It happens to almost everyone. A trusted friend shares your secret, talks behind your back, or drops you for a new crowd. Coach your teen:

• 'You have a right to feel hurt — that was a betrayal of trust'
• 'You can't control what they did, only how you respond'
• 'Would you want to confront them directly, or let the friendship go?'
• 'What does this teach you about what you need in a friend?'

slides.heading: Responding to Gossip
slides.body:
Two strategies for when people talk:

1. Confront calmly: 'I've heard you've been saying things about me. I'd prefer if you talked to me directly.' (Takes courage, often shuts it down)

2. Rise above: Sometimes the most powerful response is no response. When you stop reacting, gossip loses its fuel.

Both are valid — help your teen choose based on the situation.

slides.heading: Forgive the Small Stuff
slides.body:
Friends will annoy each other. They'll be thoughtless, competitive, moody. Before blowing up a friendship over a single incident, ask:
• 'Is this a pattern or a one-off?'
• 'Are they going through something hard?'
• 'Is this worth losing the friendship over?'

Forgive the small quirks. Draw the line at repeated cruelty.

1. Confront calmly: 'I've heard you've been saying things about me. I'd prefer if you talked to me directly.' 2. Rise above: Sometimes the most powerful response is no response — when you stop reacting, gossip loses its fuel. Both are valid — help your teen choose based on the situation.

Friends will annoy each other — they'll be thoughtless, competitive, moody. Before ending a friendship over one incident, ask: 'Is this a pattern or a one-off?' 'Are they going through something hard?' 'Is this worth losing the friendship over?' Forgive quirks. Draw the line at repeated cruelty.

cards.front: When to Step In as a Parent
cards.back: For most teen friendship dramas, coach your child to handle it themselves. Only step in when: there's persistent bullying, there are safety concerns, or the school needs to be involved. Premature parent involvement usually makes social situations worse.

content.question: How well do you think your child models being a genuinely good friend to others?

slides.heading: The Emotional Bank Account
slides.body:
Every relationship has an invisible 'trust bank account'. Deposits: keeping promises, being kind, listening, showing up. Withdrawals: gossip, flaking, selfishness, breaking trust.

When the account is full, friendships can survive tough moments. When it's empty, one small conflict can end it.

Ask your teen: 'Are you making more deposits or withdrawals in your friendships?'

slides.heading: Listen First
slides.body:
The #1 friendship skill: genuinely listening. Not waiting for your turn to talk. Not looking at your phone. Actually hearing what someone is feeling.

Practice at home:
• 'Tell me about your day — I'm just going to listen'
• Model putting your phone down during conversations
• Reflect back: 'It sounds like you felt...' before offering advice

slides.heading: Stand Up, Don't Stand By
slides.body:
A true friend doesn't just avoid being mean — they stand up when someone else IS being mean. Teach your teen:
• 'If you see someone being excluded, invite them in'
• 'If a friend is being talked about, change the subject or walk away'
• 'Being a bystander IS a choice — and it's the wrong one'

Courage in small moments builds character for big ones.

activities.title: Being a Good Friend
activities.instruction: Flip each card to discover the skills that make people genuinely want to be around you.

cards.back: Every relationship has an invisible trust bank. Deposits: keeping promises, being kind, listening, showing up. Withdrawals: gossip, flaking, selfishness, breaking trust. When the account is full, friendships survive tough moments. When it's empty, one small conflict can end everything.

The number-one friendship skill is genuinely listening — not waiting for your turn to talk, not looking at your phone, but actually hearing what someone is feeling. Practise at home: put phones down, reflect back 'It sounds like you felt...' before offering any advice.

A true friend doesn't just avoid being mean — they stand up when someone else IS being mean. If you see someone being excluded, invite them in. If a friend is being talked about, change the subject or walk away. Being a bystander IS a choice — and it's the wrong one.

Standing up for someone takes courage every time. But courage in small moments (defending someone in conversation, including the left-out kid) builds character for big ones. These small acts matter far more than they appear.

content.question: How confident do you feel having honest conversations with your teen about substances and addiction?

slides.heading: Truth 1: It's Progressive
slides.body:
Nobody plans to become addicted. It starts small and grows slowly. First it's fun, then it's fun with problems, then it's just problems. The teenage brain is especially vulnerable because the reward system is hypersensitive while the 'brake system' (prefrontal cortex) is still developing.

This isn't a moral failing — it's neuroscience.

slides.heading: Truth 2: Addiction Replaces Connection
slides.body:
People don't become addicted to substances — they become addicted to the relief substances provide. Loneliness, anxiety, boredom, pain — substances numb these. The antidote isn't willpower — it's CONNECTION.

The strongest protective factor against addiction: a teen who feels genuinely connected to their family and has at least one trusted adult they can talk to.

slides.heading: Truth 3: It Can Happen to Anyone
slides.body:
Addiction doesn't discriminate by income, intelligence, or family type. Risk factors include:
• Family history of addiction
• Untreated anxiety or depression
• Early exposure (before age 15)
• Trauma
• Social isolation
• Peer group that normalises substance use

Protective factors: strong family bond, clear boundaries, emotional literacy, meaningful activities, delayed first exposure.

activities.title: Three Truths About Addiction
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the key facts every parent and teen needs to know.

cards.back: Nobody plans to become addicted. It starts small: first it's fun, then it's fun with problems, then it's just problems. The teenage brain's reward system is hypersensitive while the prefrontal 'brake system' is still developing — making teens uniquely vulnerable. This is neuroscience, not moral failure.

People don't become addicted to substances — they become addicted to the RELIEF substances provide: from loneliness, anxiety, boredom, or pain. The antidote isn't willpower — it's connection. The strongest protective factor: a teen who feels genuinely connected to family and has a trusted adult.

Risk factors: family history of addiction, untreated anxiety or depression, early exposure (before 15), trauma, social isolation, peer group that normalises use. Protective factors: strong family bond, clear values, emotional literacy, meaningful activities, delayed first exposure.

Cannabis is not safe for teenagers. Regular use before age 25 can impair memory, motivation, and attention, and increase psychosis risk in those predisposed. The developing brain is uniquely vulnerable. 'Natural' does not mean safe for a brain under construction.

content.explanation: Cannabis significantly affects the developing teenage brain. Research shows regular use before age 25 can impair memory, motivation, attention, and increase risk of psychosis in those predisposed. 'Natural' does not mean safe for a developing brain.

questions.question: What is identified as the strongest protective factor against teen substance abuse?
options: Strict rules and consequences
Zero-tolerance policies at school
A teen who feels genuinely connected to family and has at least one trusted adult
Keeping teens busy with activities
questions.explanation: Connection is the antidote to addiction. Teens who feel genuinely loved, known, and connected — and who have a trusted adult they can talk to — are dramatically less likely to turn to substances to manage difficult emotions.

questions.question: Addiction is best understood as:
options: A moral failing that reflects poor character
A choice that teenagers make when they're bored
Progressive dependence that starts small and grows, often driven by a need to escape emotional pain
Something that only happens to children from difficult families
questions.explanation: Addiction is progressive — nobody plans to become dependent. It starts as relief (from pain, loneliness, anxiety) and gradually becomes the main problem. It's a neurological and psychological process, not a character flaw.

questions.question: Which of the following is a PROTECTIVE factor against addiction?
options: Early exposure to alcohol 'to teach moderation'
Keeping substance conversations off-limits
Meaningful activities and emotional literacy
Highly permissive parenting
questions.explanation: Protective factors include: strong family bonds, clear values, emotional literacy, meaningful activities (sport, creative work, volunteering), and delayed first exposure to substances. These build resilience against the pull of addictive coping.

content.question: How concerned are you about your child's current relationship with screens and social media?

slides.heading: The Dopamine Loop
slides.body:
Social media, gaming, and short-form video are engineered to be addictive. Every notification, like, and new video triggers a dopamine hit in your teen's already-sensitive reward system.

Signs of dependency:
• Anxiety when phone is taken away
• Can't go 10 minutes without checking
• Mood crashes after scrolling
• Choosing screen over real-life activities
• Sleep disruption from late-night use

slides.heading: Boundaries That Work
slides.body:
Negotiate boundaries WITH them (not imposed on them):
• No phones at meals or in bedrooms after a set time
• Screen-free first hour after waking
• Weekly screen time review together (not as punishment — as awareness)
• Model it yourself (if you're always on YOUR phone, why shouldn't they be?)
• Replace screen time with something better, not just nothing

slides.heading: The Comparison Trap
slides.body:
Social media creates a distorted mirror. Everyone's life looks better, easier, more exciting. Help your teen see:
• 'People post their highlights, not their hard days'
• 'How do you feel AFTER 30 minutes of scrolling? Better or worse?'
• 'What would you have done with that hour if you didn't have a phone?'

Awareness is the first step. Don't lecture — help them notice the pattern themselves.

Negotiate boundaries WITH your teen, not impose them on them. No phones at meals or in bedrooms after a set time. Screen-free first hour after waking. Weekly screen time review together. Model it yourself — if you're always on your phone, why shouldn't they be?

Removing screen time without replacing it with something better creates resentment, not change. Replace with connection, physical activity, creative projects, or outdoor time. The goal is to make healthy alternatives as accessible and appealing as screens.

questions.question: Why are social media and short-form video particularly addictive for teenagers?
options: Teenagers have poor self-control
They're engineered to trigger dopamine responses in an already hypersensitive teenage reward system
Teenagers are bored and have nothing else to do
Parents don't set enough rules
questions.explanation: Platforms are deliberately designed to maximise engagement through dopamine feedback loops — notifications, likes, infinite scroll. For the teenage brain (with a highly sensitive reward system), this engineering creates powerful dependency.

questions.question: What makes screen boundaries more likely to stick?
options: Making rules without discussion
Negotiating them WITH your teen, applying them to everyone including parents
Removing all devices immediately
Using parental controls without explanation
questions.explanation: Boundaries negotiated WITH teens have more buy-in than rules imposed on them. Applying the same rules to yourself as a parent eliminates the 'do as I say, not as I do' contradiction that teenagers quickly identify and resent.

questions.question: What does the social media 'comparison trap' do to teenagers?
options: It motivates them to do better
It creates a distorted view where everyone else's life seems better, causing anxiety and lowered self-worth
It has no real effect if parents talk to them enough
It only affects girls
questions.explanation: Social media presents highlight reels as normal life. Constant comparison to curated content erodes self-worth, creates anxiety about missing out, and generates a distorted sense of how other people actually live.

questions.question: When setting screen time limits, what should you do alongside removing screen time?
options: Nothing — the removal itself is enough
Replace it with something better, not just with nothing
Explain why screens are dangerous
Monitor their digital activity closely
questions.explanation: Removing screen time without replacing it with engaging alternatives creates resistance and resentment. The goal is to make healthy options — connection, activity, creativity — as accessible and rewarding as screens, not just to eliminate the problematic behaviour.

content.question: How well do you think you understand the emotional needs driving any unhealthy coping habits your child may have?

slides.heading: Ask Why, Not What
slides.body:
Instead of focusing on WHAT they're doing (drinking, vaping, endless scrolling), ask WHY:
• What are they trying to escape from?
• What emotion are they trying to manage?
• What need is being met by this behaviour?

'I'm not asking to judge — I'm asking because I care about what's driving this.'

slides.heading: Build Alternative Coping
slides.body:
Your teen needs healthy ways to handle:
• Stress → physical activity, breathing, journaling
• Loneliness → genuine connection, community, pets
• Boredom → creative projects, nature, learning something new
• Pain → therapy, talking, processing with a safe adult

The goal: make healthy coping as accessible and rewarding as the unhealthy option.

slides.heading: If They're Already Struggling
slides.body:
If you suspect substance use or serious dependency:
• Don't panic publicly (process your fear with another adult first)
• Approach with care: 'I've noticed some changes. I'm worried, not angry.'
• Listen more than you talk
• Seek professional help early (GP, counsellor, addiction service)
• NZ: Alcohol Drug Helpline 0800 787 797
• Remember: early intervention dramatically improves outcomes

content.question: How would you rate your child's current level of self-worth and genuine confidence?

slides.heading: The Social Mirror
slides.body:
The 'social mirror' is what the world reflects back at your child: peer opinions, social media likes, grades, appearance comments. This mirror is distorted — it changes daily, it's based on others' insecurities, and it never gives an accurate picture.

If your child bases their worth on this mirror, they'll always be searching for validation.

slides.heading: The True Mirror
slides.body:
The 'true mirror' reflects who they actually are: their values, their effort, their kindness, their growth. This mirror is stable — it doesn't change based on who's looking.

Help them build this mirror by regularly reflecting THEIR qualities back to them:
• 'I noticed you helped that kid who was sitting alone. That takes courage.'
• 'You didn't give up on that project even when it was hard. That's persistence.'
• 'The way you handled that disagreement showed real maturity.'

slides.heading: Character + Competence
slides.body:
True confidence comes from two sources:

1. CHARACTER: Who you are when no one's watching. Integrity, kindness, resilience.
2. COMPETENCE: Getting good at something through effort. Sport, art, music, academics, cooking, fixing things.

Help your child develop BOTH. Character without skill feels hollow. Skill without character feels empty.

True confidence comes from two sources: CHARACTER (who you are when no one's watching — integrity, kindness, resilience) and COMPETENCE (getting genuinely good at something through effort). Develop both. Character without skill feels hollow. Skill without character feels empty.

content.question: How well do you think your child faces personal challenges rather than avoiding them?

slides.heading: Everyone Has One
slides.body:
Every child has something that feels like their biggest obstacle — their personal dragon to slay. It might be:
• Speaking up in class
• Making friends
• A learning difficulty
• Body image
• A family situation
• Anxiety
• Not fitting in

The size of the challenge doesn't matter. What matters is that they face it, not avoid it.

slides.heading: Small Wins Build Confidence
slides.body:
Confidence doesn't come from affirmations or pep talks. It comes from DOING hard things and surviving. Help your child:

1. Name the challenge (what specifically scares them?)
2. Break it into tiny steps
3. Celebrate each step (not just the outcome)
4. Normalise setbacks ('Everyone falls. Getting up is the skill.')
5. Model your own struggles ('I was nervous about that presentation too')

slides.heading: The Anti-Comparison Practice
slides.body:
Comparison is the thief of joy — especially for teenagers. Help them shift:

FROM: 'Why am I not as good/pretty/smart/popular as them?'
TO: 'Am I better than I was yesterday?'

Create a family practice: each person shares one thing they improved at this week, no matter how small. Progress is personal.

activities.title: Conquering Your Child's Personal Challenge
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand how to help your child face and overcome their biggest obstacle.

cards.back: Every child has something that feels like their biggest obstacle — speaking up in class, making friends, body image, a learning difficulty, anxiety. The size of the challenge doesn't matter. What matters is that they FACE it, not avoid it. Avoidance always makes things bigger.

Confidence doesn't come from affirmations or pep talks. It comes from doing hard things and surviving. Help your child: name the challenge, break it into tiny steps, celebrate each step (not just outcomes), normalise setbacks, and model your own struggles.

'Everyone falls. Getting up is the skill.' Share your own failures and how you recovered. When children see adults handle failure with resilience rather than shame, they learn that setbacks are normal — not proof that they're incapable.

FROM: 'Why am I not as good/smart/popular as them?' TO: 'Am I better than I was yesterday?' Create a family practice: each person shares one thing they improved this week, no matter how small. Progress is personal and self-referenced, not comparative.

questions.explanation: When children see adults fail and recover without shame, they learn that setbacks are survivable — not proof of being broken or incapable. Modelling recovery from failure normalises the process and demonstrates resilience in action.

content.question: How reactive do you feel you are as a parent right now — how often do you react without pausing to choose your response?

slides.heading: The Autopilot Problem
slides.body: Clarke-Fields explains that most parenting reactions are on autopilot — we default to whatever WE experienced growing up. Yelling, threatening, shaming, withdrawing — these aren't conscious choices. They're conditioned responses from our own childhood. The first step to changing is noticing: 'I'm reacting, not responding.'

slides.heading: Mapping Your Triggers
slides.body:
Common parental triggers and what's underneath:
• Child whining → 'I can't handle being needed constantly' (overwhelm)
• Child defying → 'I'm not respected/in control' (powerlessness)
• Child crying → 'I was told crying was weakness' (inherited shame)
• Sibling fighting → 'I need peace to function' (sensory overload)
• Child lying → 'I can't trust anyone' (betrayal wound)

Your trigger reveals YOUR unmet need, not your child's flaw.

slides.heading: The STOP Practice
slides.body:
When you feel the surge of reactivity:

S — Stop. Physically pause. Don't speak.
T — Take a breath. One deep breath reactivates your prefrontal cortex.
O — Observe. What am I feeling? What's my body doing? What story am I telling myself?
P — Proceed. Now choose your response consciously.

This takes 10 seconds. Those 10 seconds change everything.

slides.heading: Repair Over Perfection
slides.body:
You WILL lose it sometimes. Clarke-Fields says the magic isn't in never making mistakes — it's in how you repair. After you've calmed down:
• 'I yelled at you and that wasn't okay. I'm sorry.'
• 'You didn't deserve that. I was feeling overwhelmed and I handled it badly.'
• 'What can I do to make this right?'

Repair teaches your child: mistakes are human, accountability matters, and relationships can heal.

content.question: How aware are you of generational parenting patterns you might be unconsciously repeating?

slides.heading: The Inheritance
slides.body: Clarke-Fields is clear: we parent the way we were parented UNLESS we consciously choose otherwise. The phrases that come out under stress — 'Because I said so,' 'Stop crying or I'll give you something to cry about,' 'You're being ridiculous' — those are echoes. They're your parents' voices coming through your mouth. Noticing this is the beginning of change.

slides.heading: The Inner Child Work
slides.body: When your child's behaviour triggers an outsized reaction, ask: 'How old do I feel right now?' Often the answer isn't your actual age — it's 6, or 10, or 14. Your wounded inner child is reacting to their wounded inner child. Two hurt kids can't solve anything. The adult needs to show up first.

slides.heading: Choosing Your Legacy
slides.body:
Write two lists:
1. What I received from my parents that I want to KEEP: (love of reading, family dinners, work ethic...)
2. What I received that I want to CHANGE: (criticism, emotional unavailability, yelling, comparison...)

You are the transition generation. The patterns that stop with you don't reach your grandchildren.

slides.heading: Daily Mindfulness Practice
slides.body:
Clarke-Fields recommends just 5 minutes daily:
• Morning: set a parenting intention ('Today I will pause before reacting')
• During conflict: one conscious breath before speaking
• Evening: reflect without judgment — 'What went well? What would I do differently?'

Mindfulness isn't about being calm all the time. It's about being AWARE of when you're not calm — and choosing what to do next.

slides.heading: Instead of Yelling
slides.body:
REACTIVE: 'HOW MANY TIMES DO I HAVE TO TELL YOU?!'
RESPONSIVE: 'I notice this keeps happening. Let's figure out a system that works for both of us.'

REACTIVE: 'STOP IT RIGHT NOW!'
RESPONSIVE: 'I can see you're struggling. I'm going to take a breath, and then we'll work this out.'

slides.body:
REACTIVE: 'What is WRONG with you?'
RESPONSIVE: 'That behaviour isn't okay. You're a good person having a hard moment.'

REACTIVE: 'You always do this!'
RESPONSIVE: 'This happened today. What was going on for you?'

REACTIVE: 'You're being such a brat!'
RESPONSIVE: 'I can see big feelings are in charge right now. I'm here when you're ready.'

slides.heading: Instead of Threatening
slides.body:
REACTIVE: 'If you don't stop, I'm taking everything away!'
RESPONSIVE: 'Here's what's going to happen: [clear, calm consequence]. You choose.'

REACTIVE: 'Wait till your father gets home!'
RESPONSIVE: 'We're going to deal with this now, together, calmly.'

The principle: consequences should be related, respectful, and reasonable — not punitive.

slides.heading: The 24-Hour Rule
slides.body:
Clarke-Fields suggests: for any non-urgent issue, wait 24 hours before having the conversation. Most things feel less catastrophic after sleep. You'll be calmer, they'll be calmer, and the conversation will be productive rather than punitive.

Exceptions: safety issues require immediate action. Everything else can wait.

activities.title: Responding vs Reacting: Scripts That Work
activities.instruction: Flip each card to learn the shift from reactive to responsive parenting language.

cards.back: REACTIVE: 'HOW MANY TIMES DO I HAVE TO TELL YOU?!' RESPONSIVE: 'I notice this keeps happening. Let's figure out a system that works for both of us.' The shift: from controlling THEM to regulating YOURSELF.

REACTIVE: 'What is WRONG with you?' RESPONSIVE: 'That behaviour isn't okay. You're a good person having a hard moment.' REACTIVE: 'You always do this!' RESPONSIVE: 'This happened today. What was going on for you?'

REACTIVE: 'If you don't stop, I'm taking everything away!' RESPONSIVE: 'Here's what's going to happen: [clear, calm consequence]. You choose.' Consequences should be related, respectful, and reasonable — not punitive.

For any non-urgent issue, wait 24 hours before having the conversation. Most things feel less catastrophic after sleep. You'll be calmer, they'll be calmer, and the conversation will be productive rather than punitive. Exception: safety issues require immediate action.

activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of mindful responses in challenging parenting moments.

questions.question: What is the key shift in 'responding instead of reacting' when you feel the urge to yell?
options: Speak more quietly
Shift from trying to control your child's behaviour to regulating your own state first
Send them to their room to cool down
Explain your feelings calmly
questions.explanation: The shift is internal — from trying to control the child (which escalates) to managing your own emotional state (which de-escalates). When you regulate yourself first, you model exactly what you're asking your child to do.

questions.question: How should you reframe 'What is WRONG with you?' in responsive parenting?
options: 'Why are you always like this?'
'I'm very disappointed in you'
'That behaviour isn't okay — and you're a good person having a hard moment'
'Go to your room and think about what you've done'
questions.explanation: This response separates the behaviour (not okay) from the person (still good). It names the issue without attacking identity — which is the foundation of discipline that teaches rather than shames.

questions.question: What principle should guide consequences in responsive parenting?
options: They should be as severe as possible to deter future behaviour
They should be related, respectful, and reasonable — not punitive
They should be decided in the heat of the moment
Consequences aren't needed if you talk enough
questions.explanation: Clarke-Fields and other gentle discipline experts agree: consequences are most effective when related to the behaviour, respectful of the child's dignity, and reasonable for their age. Punitive consequences may stop behaviour short-term but don't teach.

questions.question: When does the 24-Hour Rule NOT apply?
options: When the child is a teenager
When you're angry
When there are safety concerns requiring immediate action
When the child has broken a rule before
questions.explanation: The 24-hour rule — waiting before non-urgent conversations — applies to most discipline situations. Safety concerns (a child in danger, immediate risk) require immediate action. Everything else benefits from the calm perspective that comes after sleep.

content.prompt: Think of the last time you reacted instead of responded. Rewrite the moment: what did you say, and what could you have said instead? How might the outcome have changed?

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How do you feel about your current approach to discipline — do you feel it's teaching your child or mainly controlling them?

slides.heading: Punishment vs Discipline
slides.body:
Ockwell-Smith draws a critical distinction:

PUNISHMENT: Making a child suffer for a mistake. Goal: compliance through fear.
DISCIPLINE: Teaching a child to make better choices. Goal: understanding through connection.

Punishment stops behaviour in the moment. Discipline changes behaviour for life. The question isn't 'How do I make them stop?' — it's 'What do I want them to LEARN?'

slides.heading: Why Time-Outs Often Fail
slides.body:
Traditional time-outs isolate a dysregulated child — exactly when they need connection most. Ockwell-Smith explains that when a child is in fight/flight, their learning brain is offline. They can't reflect on what they did wrong from a 'naughty step.' They can only feel rejected.

Alternative: 'Time-IN' — sit with them, help them calm, THEN discuss what happened.

slides.heading: The Punishment-Rebellion Cycle
slides.body:
Research shows punishment creates one of three outcomes:
1. Compliance through fear (breaks the relationship)
2. Sneakiness (they learn to not get caught)
3. Rebellion (they push back harder)

None of these teach the child to make good decisions when you're not watching. Gentle discipline builds INTERNAL motivation — they do the right thing because they understand WHY, not because they're afraid.

slides.heading: Behaviour Is Communication
slides.body:
Every challenging behaviour is trying to tell you something:
• Hitting = 'I don't have words for how I feel'
• Whining = 'I need connection/attention'
• Defiance = 'I need some control over my life'
• Lying = 'I don't feel safe telling the truth'
• Tantrums = 'My feelings are too big for my body'

Address the NEED underneath the behaviour, not just the behaviour itself.

activities.title: Why Punishment Doesn't Work
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand the science of discipline versus punishment.

cards.back: PUNISHMENT: Making a child suffer for a mistake. Goal — compliance through fear. DISCIPLINE: Teaching a child to make better choices. Goal — understanding through connection. Punishment stops behaviour in the moment. Discipline changes behaviour for life.

Isolating a dysregulated child is exactly when they need connection most. When a child is in fight/flight, their learning brain is offline — they can't reflect from a 'naughty step.' They can only feel rejected. Alternative: 'Time-IN' — sit with them, help them calm, THEN discuss what happened.

Research shows punishment creates one of three outcomes: compliance through fear (breaks the relationship), sneakiness (they learn not to get caught), or rebellion (they push back harder). None of these teach good decisions when you're not watching.

Every challenging behaviour is trying to tell you something. Hitting = 'I don't have words for this feeling.' Whining = 'I need connection.' Defiance = 'I need some control.' Lying = 'I don't feel safe telling the truth.' Address the NEED underneath.

content.question: Your 4-year-old hits their sibling. According to gentle discipline, the FIRST step is:

options.label: Take away a toy as consequence
Ensure the hurt child is safe, then connect with the hitter to understand what happened
Ignore it — they'll grow out of it

content.explanation: Gentle discipline prioritises safety first (check on the hurt child), then connection (what's going on for the child who hit?), then teaching ('Hitting hurts. When you're angry, you can....'). Punishment skips the learning step entirely.

activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of why punishment doesn't work and what to do instead.

questions.question: What is the key difference between punishment and discipline?
options: Punishment is louder; discipline is quieter
Punishment makes children suffer for mistakes; discipline teaches children to make better choices
Punishment is physical; discipline is verbal
There is no meaningful difference
questions.explanation: Punishment aims for compliance through fear. Discipline aims to teach through connection and understanding. Punishment may stop behaviour immediately but doesn't create internal motivation to behave well when unsupervised.

questions.question: Why do traditional time-outs often fail for young children?
options: They're too comfortable
Children enjoy the alone time
They isolate a dysregulated child exactly when they need connection most — and a brain in fight/flight cannot reflect and learn
They're not long enough
questions.explanation: When a child is dysregulated (in fight/flight mode), their thinking brain is offline. They cannot reflect from a naughty step — they can only feel abandoned and rejected. A 'time-in' (sitting with them calmly until they regulate) then discussing what happened is more effective.

questions.question: When a child hits, gentle discipline says the underlying message is often:
options: They are naturally aggressive
'I don't have words for how I feel right now'
'I want to hurt my sibling'
'I need stricter consequences'
questions.explanation: Challenging behaviours communicate unmet needs or underdeveloped skills. Hitting usually means the child doesn't have emotional vocabulary or coping strategies yet. Addressing the need (teaching emotional expression) is more effective than punishing the behaviour.

questions.question: What are the three typical outcomes of punishment-based discipline?
options: Learning, understanding, and change
Compliance through fear, sneakiness, or rebellion — none of which teach good decisions
Remorse, apology, and improvement
Immediate change, long-term change, or no change
questions.explanation: Research consistently shows punishment creates compliance through fear (damages relationship), sneakiness (learns to hide behaviour), or rebellion (escalates defiance). None builds the internal motivation to make good choices independently.

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How often do you find yourself expecting your child to do things they're developmentally not yet capable of?

slides.heading: The Immature Brain
slides.body:
Ockwell-Smith emphasises: most 'misbehaviour' is developmentally NORMAL. A 2-year-old grabbing toys isn't 'selfish' — they haven't developed theory of mind yet. A 5-year-old lying isn't 'manipulative' — they're testing reality. A teenager slamming doors isn't 'disrespectful' — their emotional regulation is under construction.

Matching expectations to brain development prevents frustration on both sides.

slides.heading: What to Expect & When
slides.body:
0–2: Cannot share, cannot regulate emotions, cannot understand 'why'
2–4: Beginning empathy, short impulse control, emotional flooding common
4–7: Can follow rules but will forget under stress, developing conscience
7–11: Can reason, understand consequences, still emotionally immature
12+: Can think abstractly but prefrontal cortex still developing until ~25

Ask: 'Is this something my child CAN'T do yet, or WON'T do?'

slides.heading: Reframing Challenging Phases
slides.body:
• 'Terrible twos' → 'The age of autonomy' (they're learning independence)
• 'Threenager' → 'The age of imagination' (testing boundaries = testing reality)
• 'Difficult tween' → 'The age of identity' (they're figuring out who they are)
• 'Impossible teenager' → 'The age of separation' (biologically designed to pull away)

Every frustrating phase serves a developmental purpose.

activities.title: Age-Appropriate Expectations
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand what children's developing brains can actually do at each stage.

cards.back: Most 'misbehaviour' is developmentally NORMAL. A 2-year-old grabbing toys isn't selfish — they haven't developed theory of mind yet. A 5-year-old lying isn't manipulative — they're testing reality. Matching expectations to brain development prevents frustration on both sides.

0–2: Cannot share, cannot regulate emotions. 2–4: Beginning empathy, short impulse control, emotional flooding. 4–7: Can follow rules but forgets under stress. 7–11: Can reason, still emotionally immature. 12+: Can think abstractly, but prefrontal cortex still developing until ~25.

Before disciplining, ask: 'Is this something my child CAN'T do yet, or WON'T do?' A child who can't share at age 2 needs teaching, not punishment. A child who won't share at age 7 needs a different conversation. The distinction changes your response completely.

'Terrible twos' → Age of autonomy (learning independence). 'Threenager' → Age of imagination (testing reality). 'Difficult tween' → Age of identity (figuring out who they are). 'Impossible teenager' → Age of separation (biologically designed to pull away). Every frustrating phase serves a purpose.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of age-appropriate expectations in discipline.

questions.question: Why is a 2-year-old grabbing toys NOT a sign of bad character?
options: It is a sign of bad character that needs discipline
2-year-olds haven't developed theory of mind yet — sharing requires understanding other people's feelings
They need more socialisation
Parents are being too permissive
questions.explanation: Theory of mind — the ability to understand that others have different thoughts and feelings — develops gradually between ages 3–5. Expecting a 2-year-old to share willingly means expecting a cognitive capacity they don't yet have.

questions.question: The key question before disciplining a child is:
options: 'How many times have I told them?'
'What consequence should I use?'
'Is this something they CAN'T do yet, or WON'T do?'
'What would other parents think?'
questions.explanation: Can't vs Won't is the crucial distinction. A child who literally cannot do something yet (due to brain development) needs teaching and support. A child who won't (choosing not to despite being capable) needs a different kind of engagement.

questions.question: When is a teenager's prefrontal cortex (the reasoning, impulse-control brain) fully developed?
options: At age 13
At age 16
At age 18
Around age 25
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex — responsible for impulse control, long-term planning, and rational decision-making — isn't fully developed until approximately age 25. This is why teenage behaviour that looks 'unreasonable' to adults is often literally still developing.

questions.question: Ockwell-Smith reframes the 'terrible twos' as:
options: A period of poor parenting outcomes
The 'age of autonomy' — when children are learning independence
A phase that can be avoided with consistent discipline
Evidence that children need stricter boundaries
questions.explanation: The 'terrible twos' reflect a child discovering autonomy and independence — a healthy, essential developmental stage. Reframing challenging phases as developmentally purposeful reduces parent frustration and promotes more effective, patient responses.

content.sentence: After losing your temper, say: 'I ___ at you and that wasn't okay. I'm ___. You didn't ___ that. I was feeling ___ and I handled it badly.'

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How confident are you in setting firm, loving boundaries WITHOUT resorting to threats or punishment?

slides.heading: Natural & Logical Consequences
slides.body:
Natural consequences: 'You didn't wear your coat → you got cold' (the world teaches)
Logical consequences: 'You threw the toy → the toy is put away for today' (related, respectful, reasonable)

Ockwell-Smith's test: Is the consequence RELATED to the behaviour? Is it RESPECTFUL of the child? Is it REASONABLE for their age? If any answer is no, it's punishment disguised as a consequence.

slides.heading: The CALM Approach
slides.body:
C — Connect first. Get on their level, make eye contact, use a calm voice.
A — Acknowledge the feeling. 'I can see you're really frustrated.'
L — Limit the behaviour. 'I won't let you hit. Hitting hurts.'
M — Move to solution. 'What could you do instead when you feel this angry?'

This takes longer than yelling. But the learning lasts infinitely longer.

slides.heading: Collaborative Problem-Solving
slides.body:
For recurring issues, sit down OUTSIDE the moment and problem-solve together:
1. 'I've noticed mornings are really stressful. What's hard about them for you?'
2. 'What's hard about them for me is...'
3. 'What could we try that works for both of us?'
4. Write the plan together. Try it for a week. Review.

Children who help create solutions are far more likely to follow them.

slides.heading: When You Need to Say No
slides.body:
Gentle doesn't mean permissive. You CAN say no firmly and kindly:
• 'I hear you want to stay up. The answer is no. Your body needs sleep.'
• 'I understand you're disappointed. We're still leaving now.'
• 'You can feel angry about the boundary. The boundary stays.'

Hold the limit with calm confidence. Empathy for their feelings doesn't mean changing the rule.

activities.title: The Gentle Discipline Toolkit
activities.instruction: Flip each card to learn practical tools that maintain boundaries AND connection.

cards.back: Natural: 'You didn't wear your coat → you got cold.' Logical: 'You threw the toy → the toy goes away today.' Ockwell-Smith's test: Is the consequence RELATED to the behaviour? RESPECTFUL of the child? REASONABLE for their age? If any answer is no, it's punishment disguised as a consequence.

C — Connect first. Get on their level, make eye contact, use a calm voice. A — Acknowledge the feeling. 'I can see you're really frustrated.' L — Limit the behaviour. 'I won't let you hit. Hitting hurts.' M — Move to solution. 'What could you do instead when you feel this angry?'

For recurring issues, sit down OUTSIDE the moment: 'I've noticed mornings are really stressful. What's hard about them for you? What's hard for me is... What could we try that works for both of us?' Write the plan together, try it for a week, review it. Children who help create solutions follow them.

You CAN say no firmly and kindly: 'I hear you want to stay up. The answer is no. Your body needs sleep.' 'I understand you're disappointed. We're still leaving now.' 'You can feel angry about the boundary. The boundary stays.' Empathy for feelings doesn't mean changing the rule.

activities.title: Knowledge Check
activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of the gentle discipline toolkit.

questions.question: What is a logical consequence according to Ockwell-Smith?
options: Any punishment that teaches a lesson
A consequence that is related, respectful, and reasonable — connected to the actual behaviour
Time-out in the child's room
Taking away all screen time indefinitely
questions.explanation: Logical consequences must pass three tests: RELATED (connected to the behaviour, not arbitrary), RESPECTFUL (preserving the child's dignity), and REASONABLE (appropriate for their age). Consequences that fail any of these tests are simply punishments with a different name.

questions.question: In the CALM approach, what does the 'A' stand for?
options: Act calmly
Acknowledge the feeling
Ask what happened
Address the behaviour
questions.explanation: A stands for Acknowledge the feeling — 'I can see you're really frustrated.' Acknowledging the emotion BEFORE addressing the behaviour is crucial. A child who feels understood can then move into the 'L' (limit) and 'M' (move to solution) stages.

questions.question: Why are children more likely to follow solutions they helped create?
options: They feel responsible for consequences
They understand the rules better when explained
They have greater ownership and buy-in when they were part of creating the solution
They tend to be more cooperative than adults expect
questions.explanation: Collaborative problem-solving builds genuine investment in solutions. When children help identify the problem, brainstorm options, and choose an approach, they feel respected and are far more motivated to follow through.

questions.question: In gentle discipline, saying 'You can feel angry about the boundary — the boundary stays' demonstrates:
options: That parents don't care about children's feelings
That empathy for feelings can coexist with firm boundaries — gentle doesn't mean permissive
A failure to listen to the child
Poor conflict resolution
questions.explanation: One of the most important concepts in gentle discipline: validating a child's emotions does NOT mean changing your boundaries. You can fully acknowledge their anger while holding the limit firm — this models emotional regulation and boundary-setting simultaneously.

content.prompt: Think of a recurring discipline issue in your home. Using the CALM approach, write out how you could handle it differently next time. What's the feeling underneath the behaviour?

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
activities.instruction: Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.

content.question: How confident are you that your child feels they can talk to you about anything — including the hard stuff?

slides.heading: Why Kids Stop Talking
slides.body:
Faber identifies the conversation killers parents use daily without realising:
• Denying feelings: 'You're fine!' 'There's nothing to be scared of'
• Philosophising: 'Well, life isn't always fair'
• Advising: 'What you should do is...'
• Interrogating: 'Why did you do that? What were you thinking?'
• Defending the other person: 'I'm sure they didn't mean it'

Each one sends the message: your feelings aren't valid. Eventually, they stop sharing.

slides.heading: The Faber Method: Accept Feelings
slides.body:
Instead of fixing, try:
1. LISTEN with full attention (put down your phone)
2. ACKNOWLEDGE with a word: 'Oh...' 'Mmm...' 'I see...'
3. NAME the feeling: 'That sounds really frustrating'
4. GIVE the wish in fantasy: 'I wish I could make it not rain for your game'

This doesn't fix the problem. It does something better — it makes your child feel understood. A child who feels understood will come back.

slides.heading: The Power of 'Tell Me More'
slides.body:
Silverman's simplest tool: when your child mentions something — anything — say 'Tell me more about that.' Not 'why?' (feels interrogative). Not 'what happened?' (feels investigative). Just: 'Tell me more.'

This works with toddlers and teenagers. It signals genuine interest without pressure. It hands them control of the conversation. And it often reveals things you'd never have known to ask about.

activities.title: The Art of Listening: Key Concepts
activities.instruction: Flip each card to understand what makes children stop talking — and how to reopen the door.

cards.back: Faber identifies daily conversation killers: Denying feelings ('You're fine!'), philosophising ('Life isn't always fair'), advising ('What you should do is...'), interrogating ('Why? What were you thinking?'), defending the other person ('I'm sure they didn't mean it'). Each sends the message: your feelings aren't valid.

Instead of fixing, try: 1. LISTEN with full attention (phone down). 2. ACKNOWLEDGE with a word: 'Oh... Mmm... I see...' 3. NAME the feeling: 'That sounds really frustrating.' 4. GIVE the wish in fantasy: 'I wish I could make it not rain for your game.' A child who feels understood will come back.

Silverman's simplest tool: when your child mentions anything, say 'Tell me more about that.' Not 'why?' (feels interrogative). Not 'what happened?' (feels investigative). Just: 'Tell me more.' Works with toddlers and teenagers. Signals genuine interest, hands them control of the conversation.

The goal of listening isn't to fix the problem. It's to make your child feel understood. A child who feels understood will keep talking, keep coming back, and eventually let you in to help. Advice without acknowledgment is wasted — understanding first unlocks everything else.

content.question: Your child says 'Nobody at school likes me.' Best first response?

options.label: 'Of course they do! You have lots of friends!'
'That sounds really lonely. Tell me more about what happened.'
'Maybe if you were nicer to people...'
'Do you want me to talk to your teacher?'

content.explanation: Faber's approach: acknowledge the feeling first, then invite them to share more. Denying ('of course they do') invalidates. Advising and fixing skip the emotional step entirely.

activities.instruction: Test what you've learned before moving on.

content.intro: Let's check your understanding of the art of listening.

questions.question: According to Faber, what happens when parents consistently use 'conversation killers'?
options: Children become better at arguing
Children eventually stop sharing because they learn their feelings aren't valid
Children become more independent
Nothing — children always want to talk to their parents
questions.explanation: Each conversation killer — denying feelings, immediately advising, interrogating — sends the message that the child's emotional experience is invalid or unwelcome. Over time, children learn to stop sharing because sharing feels pointless or unsafe.

questions.question: In the Faber listening method, what is the FIRST step?
options: Name the feeling
Offer a solution
Listen with full attention — phone down, eyes up, body present
Ask clarifying questions
questions.explanation: The first step is undivided attention — putting the phone down, making eye contact, and being fully present. Before any words are spoken, your body language communicates whether you're genuinely interested or just going through the motions.

questions.question: Why does Silverman recommend 'Tell me more' over 'Why?' or 'What happened?'
options: It's simpler to say
'Why?' and 'What happened?' feel interrogative or investigative; 'Tell me more' signals pure interest and hands them control
Children respond better to open-ended requests
It avoids conflict
questions.explanation: 'Why?' puts children on the defensive (it implies they need to justify themselves). 'What happened?' feels like an investigation. 'Tell me more' is neutral, curious, and gives the child complete control over what they share and how.

questions.question: What is the ultimate goal of empathic listening?
options: Gathering information to give good advice
Making the child feel understood — which keeps them coming back and opens the door to eventual help
Showing the child you care
Solving their problems
questions.explanation: Feeling understood is the prerequisite for being helped. A child who feels heard will keep talking, return to you when things get difficult, and eventually be open to your input. Advice without acknowledgment lands in a closed heart.

activities.title: How Are You Feeling?
